Meridional ranks of iterated Whitehead doubles

Honghao Gao H. GaoYau Mathematical Sciences Center, Tsinghua University, Beijing, 100084 & Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications, Beijing, 101408, China Email address: gaohonghao@tsinghua.edu.cn , Shijie Gu S. GuDepartment of Mathematics, Northeastern University, Shenyang, Liaoning, China, 110004 Email address: shijiegutop@gmail.com , Zhenkun Li Z. LiState Key Laboratory of Mathematical Sciences, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China Email address: zhenkun@amss.ac.cn and Jian Wang J. WangState Key Laboratory of Mathematical Sciences, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China Email address: jian.wang.4@amss.ac.cn
Date: November 11, 2026
Abstract.

We prove that every iterated untwisted Whitehead double of a nontrivial two-bridge knot satisfies the meridional rank conjecture. More precisely, for such a knot KK and every N≥0N\geq 0, the augmentation rank, meridional rank, and bridge number of WhN⁡(K)\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K) are all 2N+12^{N+1}. We use microlocal sheaf theory and a doubling construction to produce a lower bound for the meridional rank of the Whitehead double, assuming the peripheral data satisfy suitable conditions. For two-bridge knots, the required curves arise from ideal points detecting nonzero boundary slopes. In contrast, the ordinary group rank of an NN-fold Whitehead double is at most the rank of the companion group plus NN. We also give a non-example when the doubling construction does not work – the first Whitehead double of the square knot has augmentation rank at most 5, whereas its meridional rank and bridge number are 6.

Key words and phrases: 
Meridional rank, Whitehead doubles, bridge number, augmentation rank, knot contact homology, two-bridge knots, character varieties, boundary slopes

1. Introduction

Let K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} be a knot and let πK=π1​(S3∖K)\pi_{K}=\pi_{1}(S^{3}\setminus K). The meridional rank mr⁡(K)\operatorname{mr}(K) is the minimum number of meridians needed to generate πK\pi_{K}. A bridge presentation gives a meridional generating set, so mr⁡(K)≤b⁡(K)\operatorname{mr}(K)\leq b(K), where b⁡(K)b(K) denotes the bridge number. The meridional rank conjecture of Cappell–Shaneson asks whether equality holds for every knot. It appears in Kirby’s problem list [27, Problem 1.11] and, in its link formulation. See also [3, Problem 1.18(a)].

The conjecture is known for several classes of knots and links. Boileau–Zieschang proved it for Montesinos links by using their twofold branched covers [10], and Rost–Zieschang proved it for torus links [31]. The characterization of knots whose groups can be generated by two meridians is due to Boileau–Zimmermann [11, Corollary 3.3], together with the subsequent orbifold geometrization theorem [9].

Diagrammatic descriptions of bridge number clarify a difficulty in the conjecture. Blair–Kjuchukova–Velazquez–Villanueva [6] proved that the bridge number equals the Wirtinger number, the minimum number of seed strands needed for successive Wirtinger generation over all diagrams. Blair–Kjuchukova–Pfaff allow relations witnessed by certain embedded two-spheres; their plain sphere number also equals the bridge number [5]. To deduce the conjecture from these descriptions, one would still need to pass from an arbitrary meridional generating set to such a system without increasing its size.

For lower bounds, the conjugacy class of a meridian is essential. Ordinary group rank gr⁡(K)\operatorname{gr}(K) allows arbitrary generators and can be much smaller: a nontrivial torus-knot group has rank two, whereas its meridional rank can be arbitrarily large [31]. A quotient retaining the meridian class can give a stronger bound. Baader–Blair–Kjuchukova use meridian-to-reflection Coxeter quotients to prove the conjecture for twisted links and arborescent links associated to bipartite trees with nonzero even weights [1]. Baader–Kjuchukova [2, Section 2] use symmetric-group quotients to prove the meridional rank conjecture for a family of twisted Whitehead doubles of connected sums of T⁡(2,5)T(2,5), with arbitrarily large bridge number. Recent work of Blair–Kjuchukova–Pfaff extends this approach to fishnet families with any prescribed bridge number at least three and arbitrarily large bridge distance relative to that number [4]. The question of what finite quotients can detect is also recorded in [3, Problem 1.18(b)].

Knot contact homology gives a different lower bound. Cornwell [16, Theorems 1.2 and 1.5] relates its augmentations to representations of the knot group and proves

(1.1) ar⁡(K)≤mr⁡(K)≤b⁡(K),\operatorname{ar}(K)\leq\operatorname{mr}(K)\leq b(K),

where ar⁡(K)\operatorname{ar}(K) denotes augmentation rank. In the corresponding microlocal rank one representations, a meridian acts by a diagonalizable rank-one perturbation of the identity. For an irreducible microlocal rank one representation ρ\rho, the images of ρ⁡(mi)−I\rho(m_{i})-I for any meridional generating set {mi}\{m_{i}\} span the representation space. Its dimension, therefore, bounds the meridional rank from below. We will vary these representations and their peripheral eigenvalues along an algebraic curve to choose data for successive Whitehead doubles. We recall the definitions in Section 2.1.

We study these ranks under untwisted Whitehead doubling. Two satellite results are particularly relevant. For satellites with braid patterns, Cornwell–Hemminger prove a maximal augmentation-rank multiplication theorem and apply it to the iterated torus knots satisfying their hypotheses [15, Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 1.3]. The Whitehead pattern has winding number zero, so that theorem does not apply directly. Using the action on the tree associated to a satellite decomposition, Boileau–Dutra–Jang–Weidmann control the peripheral intersections of meridional subgroups. They prove the conjecture for the class generated from meridionally tame knots by connected sums and satellites with braid patterns [7, Theorem 1]. This includes every knot whose exterior is a graph manifold [7, Corollary 1]. However, Whitehead doubles of nontrivial knots are not meridionally tame [7, Introduction and Section 6], so this theorem does not directly include Whitehead iteration.

Dutra’s preprint [18, Theorem 1.1] states the meridional rank conjecture for (once) Whitehead doubles of prime algebraically tame knots. Even with this conclusion, iteration would require a new argument: the first Whitehead double is no longer algebraically tame [18, Example 2.8].11 1 There is also an issue in the pattern-subgroup argument of arXiv:2212.13081v1. In the notation on p. 7 of that version, mV=x2​x1−1​x2−1​x1=α⁡(y1​y2)=ω⁡(y1​y2)m_{V}=x_{2}x_{1}^{-1}x_{2}^{-1}x_{1}=\alpha(y_{1}y_{2})=\omega(y_{1}y_{2}) is a nontrivial element of Uα∩UωU_{\alpha}\cap U_{\omega}, contradicting Lemma 3.1 with g=1g=1. That lemma is used in the proof of Lemma 3.8(2). This identifies a gap in the argument, not a counterexample to the conclusion of Theorem 1.1. Our proof does not use these subgroup lemmas. Our contribution is a sheaf-level doubling construction whose iteration is controlled on peripheral curves realized by the companion. By keeping track of both peripheral eigenvalues, we can choose representations for which every required doubling step is defined.

Throughout, Wh⁡(K)\operatorname{Wh}(K) denotes the untwisted Whitehead double with the pattern and peripheral conventions fixed in Section 2.2. We set Wh0⁡(K)=K\operatorname{Wh}^{0}(K)=K and WhN+1⁡(K)=Wh⁡(WhN⁡(K))\operatorname{Wh}^{N+1}(K)=\operatorname{Wh}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K)). For a nontrivial companion,

(1.2) b⁡(Wh⁡(K))=2​b​(K);b(\operatorname{Wh}(K))=2b(K);

see [18, Section 4]. Thus, an augmentation rank lower bound that doubles at every step proves the meridional rank conjecture for the iterates, provided the initial augmentation rank equals b⁡(K)b(K).

1.1. Main results

Our first main result applies to every nontrivial two-bridge knot.

Theorem 1.1.

Let KK be a nontrivial two-bridge knot. For every integer N≥0N\geq 0,

ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))=mr⁡(WhN⁡(K))=b⁡(WhN⁡(K))=2N+1.\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=\operatorname{mr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=b(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=2^{N+1}.

For N=1N=1, the meridional-rank equality already follows from the lower bound for prime satellite knots in [8, Corollary 1.6]; see also [7, Introduction]. Theorem 1.1 also provides maximal-rank augmentations and propagates both equalities through every finite number of Whitehead doubles.

Given an irreducible microlocal rank one representation ρ\rho on VV, we extend ρ⊕ρ∗\rho\oplus\rho^{*} from the companion group to the satellite group, where (V∗,ρ∗)(V^{*},\rho^{*}) is the dual representation. The two distinguished peripheral eigenlines span a two-dimensional subspace of V⊕V∗V\oplus V^{*}, on which we solve the Whitehead-pattern relations explicitly. The remaining subspace is fixed by the two pattern meridians. Under the nonvanishing conditions of Theorem 2.12, this gives an irreducible 2​dimV2\dim V-dimensional representation whose meridian still has microlocal rank 11, doubling the resulting lower bound for meridional rank.

To iterate, we compute the output longitude eigenvalue as well, so that the output of one step can be tested against the hypotheses of the next. This gives the algebraic correspondence of Section 2.4. We must then find peripheral values realized by a fixed companion that admits any prescribed finite number of steps.

The difficulty is that the peripheral values realized by a fixed knot might all lie in the exceptional locus. An open dense set in the full peripheral torus does not rule this out. We address this issue using a branch at infinity of the curve. The branch is called Whitehead-iterable branch if the meridian eigenvalue has a pole and the squared longitude eigenvalue either has a pole or has a zero of order greater than that pole order; see Definition 4.1. The key observation is that one branch of the doubling correspondence again satisfies this condition. By Theorem 4.2, for each N≥0N\geq 0 there is a nonempty Zariski-open subset of the curve on which NN doubling steps can be performed. For two-bridge knots, the ideal-point argument in Section 4.2 supplies a curve with an iterable branch whose peripheral values are realized by rank-two augmentations on a Zariski-dense subset. Combining these facts with (1.1) and (1.2) proves Theorem 1.1.

The same construction provides a comparison with ordinary group rank. We call an irreducible curve in the peripheral torus an actual rank-dd augmentation peripheral curve if a Zariski-dense subset of its points is realized by rank-dd augmentations with ϵ⁡(μ)≠1\epsilon(\mu)\neq 1. The coordinates are (μ,λ2)(\mu,\lambda^{2}), where λ\lambda is the preferred longitude eigenvalue; see Definition 4.4.

Theorem 1.2.

For every knot KK and every integer N≥0N\geq 0,

gr⁡(WhN⁡(K))≤gr⁡(K)+N.\operatorname{gr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\leq\operatorname{gr}(K)+N.

If KK has an actual rank-dd augmentation peripheral curve with an iterable branch, then

ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))≥2N​d\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\geq 2^{N}d

for every N≥0N\geq 0. In particular,

gr⁡(WhN⁡(K))≤ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))whenevergr⁡(K)+N≤2N​d.\operatorname{gr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\leq\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\quad\text{whenever}\quad\operatorname{gr}(K)+N\leq 2^{N}d.

For a nontrivial two-bridge knot, this gives

gr⁡(WhN⁡(K))≤N+2≤ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))=2N+1.\operatorname{gr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\leq N+2\leq\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=2^{N+1}.

The proof is given in Section 5. A complementary lower bound for ordinary group rank was obtained by Gu–Wang–Zou [21, Proposition 1.3]. For every nontrivial knot KK and N≥1N\geq 1, their estimate and Theorem 1.2 give

N+1≤gr⁡(WhN⁡(K))≤N+gr⁡(K).N+1\leq\operatorname{gr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\leq N+\operatorname{gr}(K).

Thus ordinary group rank grows linearly, whereas the augmentation and meridional ranks in Theorem 1.1 grow exponentially. The lower bound in [21] uses the hyperbolic pieces of the JSJ decomposition and holds without an augmentation hypothesis. That work also determines ordinary group rank exactly for hyperbolic two-bridge companions; see Section 5.

The augmentation lower bound is not always sharp; this limitation is already present in Cornwell’s work [16]. Our last main result exhibits a further obstruction to iteration: even when the augmentation rank agrees with the bridge number for the companion, it may fail to double. The example nevertheless satisfies the meridional rank conjecture.

Theorem 1.3.

Let S=T⁡(2,3)​#​T⁡(2,3)¯S=T(2,3)\#\overline{T(2,3)} be the square knot. Then

ar⁡(S)=mr⁡(S)=b⁡(S)=3,\operatorname{ar}(S)=\operatorname{mr}(S)=b(S)=3,

whereas

ar⁡(Wh⁡(S))≤5<6=mr⁡(Wh⁡(S))=b⁡(Wh⁡(S)).\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}(S))\leq 5<6=\operatorname{mr}(\operatorname{Wh}(S))=b(\operatorname{Wh}(S)).

The augmentation obstruction uses the two trefoil factors of the companion group and their preferred longitudes. The meridional lower bound uses a different representation: an explicit epimorphism πWh⁡(S)→S14\pi_{\operatorname{Wh}(S)}\to S_{14} and its permutation module 𝔽214\mathbb{F}_{2}^{14}. The first cohomology of πWh⁡(S)\pi_{\operatorname{Wh}(S)} with coefficients in this module has dimension 1414, while the meridian defect has rank 33. A cocycle estimate then rules out generation by five meridians; see Section 6.2 for the representation and exact linear calculation. Here the finite quotient supplies the coefficient module for the cohomology of the knot group. This gives a strict gap between augmentation rank and meridional rank. The exact augmentation rank of Wh⁡(S)\operatorname{Wh}(S) and the ranks of further Whitehead doubles of SS remain undetermined in this paper.

1.2. Conventions and organization

All knots are oriented. A meridian is positively oriented, and elements represented by meridians are understood up to conjugacy. We use a preferred zero-linking longitude. Sheaves and augmentations may be defined over any field 𝕜\Bbbk, but in the algebraic-curve applications, we take 𝕜=ℂ\Bbbk=\mathbb{C}. The finite-dimensional permutation module in Section 6.2 is explicitly over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}.

We use πK:=π1​(S3∖K)\pi_{K}:=\pi_{1}(S^{3}\setminus K) for the knot group throughout. The commutator convention is [a,b]=a​b​a−1​b−1[a,b]=aba^{-1}b^{-1}. Products of permutations are composed from right to left, and permutation matrices act on column vectors by g​ei=eg⁡(i)ge_{i}=e_{g(i)}. The embedding ϕK\phi_{K} of the Whitehead solid torus into a tubular neighborhood of KK respects the preferred zero framing. A “two-bridge knot” in the statements below is nontrivial.

Section 2 recalls the representations and augmentations and constructs the doubling correspondence. Section 2.5 gives the meridional upper bounds. Section 3 recalls the algebraic curves, valuations, and character varieties used to find peripheral data to which the iteration applies. Section 4.1 proves the iterable-branch criterion, and Section 4.2 applies slope detection to prove Theorem 1.1. Section 5 compares ordinary group rank with augmentation rank. Finally, Section 6 proves Theorem 1.3 for the first Whitehead double of the square knot.

2. Microlocal rank-1 representations and Whitehead doubling

The meridian and the preferred longitude of a knot KK are denoted by mm and ℓ\ell, respectively. We use the specialization of knot contact homology in which the extra variable UU is set equal to one. For an embedded submanifold A⊂S3A\subset S^{3}, we denote by 𝒪​p​(A)\mathcal{O}p(A) a fixed sufficiently small open tubular neighborhood of AA.

2.1. Microlocal rank-1 representations and augmentations

We first introduce the notation for the microlocal rank of a representation of the knot group.

Definition 2.1.

For a representation ρ:πK→GL⁡(V)\rho\colon\pi_{K}\to\operatorname{GL}(V), define the microlocal rank to be

μ​rkK⁡(ρ):=rank⁡(ρ⁡(m)−I),\mu\operatorname{rk}_{K}(\rho):=\operatorname{rank}\bigl(\rho(m)-I\bigr),

where II is the identity matrix of size dimV\dim V. This number is independent of the chosen meridian, since all meridians are conjugate.

We call ρ\rho a μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation if μ​rkK​(ρ)=1\mu\operatorname{rk}_{K}(\rho)=1.

A μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation is diagonalizable if there is a basis in which

ρ⁡(m)∼diag⁡(μ,1,…,1),μ≠1.\rho(m)\sim\operatorname{diag}(\mu,1,\ldots,1),\qquad\mu\neq 1.

A μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation is unipotent if there is a basis in which

ρ⁡(m)∼(1101)⊕IdimV−2.\rho(m)\sim\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}\oplus I_{\dim V-2}.

We recall the sheaf-theoretic reason for this terminology [20, Section 3.2]. Let j:S3∖K↪S3j\colon S^{3}\setminus K\hookrightarrow S^{3} be the open embedding. A representation ρ:πK→GL⁡(V)\rho\colon\pi_{K}\to\operatorname{GL}(V) determines a local system ℰρ\mathcal{E}_{\rho} on the knot complement. For the underived direct image, the stalk of j∗​ℰρj_{*}\mathcal{E}_{\rho} on KK is the meridian-invariant subspace Vρ⁡(m)V^{\rho(m)}. The local gluing map is the inclusion

T:Vρ⁡(m)↪V.T\colon V^{\rho(m)}\hookrightarrow V.

Its mapping cone is the microlocal stalk, up to a degree shift, in the sense of Kashiwara–Schapira, along the knot conormal torus ΛK\Lambda_{K} inside the contact cosphere bundle, i.e. ΛK⊂S​T∗​S3\Lambda_{K}\subset ST^{*}S^{3} is a Legendrian surface. Consequently,

dimH∙​(Cone⁡(T))=dim(V/Vρ⁡(m))=rank⁡(ρ⁡(m)−I).\dim H^{\bullet}\!\left(\operatorname{Cone}(T)\right)=\dim(V/V^{\rho(m)})=\operatorname{rank}\bigl(\rho(m)-I\bigr).

Thus a μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation induces a microlocal rank one sheaf microsupported along the conormal. Conversely, up to the equivalence modulo local systems on S3S^{3} in [20, Definition 3.8 and Proposition 3.11], a microlocal rank one abelian sheaf comes from one of the three forms: (1) an irreducible diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-1 representation via the above construction; (2) an irreducible unipotent μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-1 representation via the above construction; and (3) a local system of rank 11 that is supported on KK [20]. The first type is generic and the main focus of this paper.

A diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation is also called a KCH representation by Cornwell [16], where KCH refers to knot contact homology. Next, we explain its background related to knot contact homology and augmentations.

The (framed) knot contact homology is a knot invariant defined via counting holomorphic disks for ΛK\Lambda_{K}, whose formula was first discovered by Ng [29]. We use the specialization U=1U=1 of the Legendrian dg algebra 𝒜⁡(ΛK)\mathcal{A}(\Lambda_{K}) associated to ΛK\Lambda_{K}. The dg algebra 𝒜⁡(ΛK)\mathcal{A}(\Lambda_{K}) is semi-freely generated by Reeb chords over ℤ⁡[H1​(ΛK)]≅ℤ⁡[μ±1,λ±1]\mathbb{Z}[H_{1}(\Lambda_{K})]\cong\mathbb{Z}[\mu^{\pm 1},\lambda^{\pm 1}]. An augmentation of the dg algebra is a morphism ϵ:𝒜⁡(ΛK)→𝕜\epsilon:\mathcal{A}(\Lambda_{K})\rightarrow\Bbbk which preserves grading, differential, and the unit. The case of the knot conormal has the special property that its generators are concentrated in non-negative degrees. Hence an augmentation descends to the degree 00 homology ϵ:H0​(𝒜⁡(ΛK))→𝕜\epsilon:H_{0}(\mathcal{A}(\Lambda_{K}))\rightarrow\Bbbk.

The algebra H0​(𝒜⁡(ΛK))H_{0}(\mathcal{A}(\Lambda_{K})) admits a combinatorial model by the framed cord algebra.

Definition 2.2.

The framed cord algebra Cord⁡(K)\operatorname{Cord}(K) is the tensor algebra over ℤ⁡[λ±1,μ±1]\mathbb{Z}[\lambda^{\pm 1},\mu^{\pm 1}] generated by symbols [γ][\gamma], γ∈πK\gamma\in\pi_{K}, modulo the following relations:

  1. (1)

    [e]=1−μ[e]=1-\mu,

  2. (2)

    [m​γ]=[γ​m]=μ⁡[γ][m\gamma]=[\gamma m]=\mu[\gamma], [ℓ​γ]=[γ​ℓ]=λ⁡[γ][\ell\gamma]=[\gamma\ell]=\lambda[\gamma],

  3. (3)

    [γ1​γ2]−[γ1​m​γ2]=[γ1]​[γ2][\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}]-[\gamma_{1}m\gamma_{2}]=[\gamma_{1}][\gamma_{2}].

An augmentation is a unital algebra homomorphism

ϵ:Cord⁡(K)⟶𝕜.\epsilon\colon\operatorname{Cord}(K)\longrightarrow\Bbbk.

Note that ϵ\epsilon includes a specialization of λ\lambda and μ\mu to nonzero elements of 𝕜\Bbbk.

Augmentations of the framed cord algebra and the above equivalence classes of microlocal rank one abelian sheaves modulo local systems are in bijective correspondence, with the normalization of [20, Theorem 4.17]. This is a theorem under the principle of “augmentation-sheaf correspondence” in the theory of Legendrian invariants. Considering the first and second cases of the sheaf classification, suppose (ρ,V)(\rho,V) is a μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-1 representation; then the associated augmentation ϵρ\epsilon_{\rho} is given by

ϵρ​([γ])=tr⁡(ρ⁡(γ)−ρ⁡(m​γ)).\epsilon_{\rho}([\gamma])=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\gamma)-\rho(m\gamma)).

Conversely, suppose ϵ\epsilon is an augmentation of the framed cord algebra with ϵ⁡(μ)≠1\epsilon(\mu)\neq 1. To reconstruct the μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-1 representation (ρϵ,Vϵ)(\rho_{\epsilon},V_{\epsilon}) following [20, Proposition 4.11], we choose a set of based meridional generators {m1,…,mN}\{m_{1},\ldots,m_{N}\} with m1=mm_{1}=m. Since the meridians are conjugate, there exist elements gi∈πKg_{i}\in\pi_{K} such that mi=gi−1​m1​gim_{i}=g_{i}^{-1}m_{1}g_{i}. Define an NN by NN square matrix RϵR_{\epsilon} by (Rϵ)i​j:=ϵ⁡([gi​gj−1])(R_{\epsilon})_{ij}:=\epsilon([g_{i}g_{j}^{-1}]). Let RjR_{j}, j=1,…,Nj=1,\ldots,N, be the column vectors of RϵR_{\epsilon}, and define the vector space

(2.1) Vϵ:=Span𝕜⁡{R1,…,RN}.V_{\epsilon}:=\operatorname{Span}_{\Bbbk}\{R_{1},\ldots,R_{N}\}.

and for any γ∈πK\gamma\in\pi_{K}, the ρϵ​(γ)\rho_{\epsilon}(\gamma) action is given by

ρϵ​(γ)​Rj:=(ϵ⁡([gi​γ​gj−1]))i=1N.\rho_{\epsilon}(\gamma)R_{j}:=\bigl(\epsilon([g_{i}\gamma g_{j}^{-1}])\bigr)_{i=1}^{N}.

The resulting representation is indeed μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-1. For example, by relation 3 in Definition 2.2,

ρϵ​(mt)​Rj=Rj−ϵ⁡([gt​gj−1])​Rt.\rho_{\epsilon}(m_{t})R_{j}=R_{j}-\epsilon([g_{t}g_{j}^{-1}])R_{t}.

It follows at once that rank⁡(ρϵ​(mt)−I)≤1\operatorname{rank}(\rho_{\epsilon}(m_{t})-I)\leq 1. Since (Rϵ)t​t=1−ϵ⁡(μ)≠0(R_{\epsilon})_{tt}=1-\epsilon(\mu)\neq 0, we have Rt≠0R_{t}\neq 0 and ρϵ​(mt)​Rt=ϵ⁡(μ)​Rt\rho_{\epsilon}(m_{t})R_{t}=\epsilon(\mu)R_{t}. Thus the rank is exactly one, and the representation is diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one. This elementary identity is the point at which the microlocal condition enters the construction.

The dimension of VϵV_{\epsilon} is independent of NN and the choices of meridional generators. Meanwhile, it does depend on the choice of ϵ\epsilon. Moreover, the representation is irreducible [16, Theorem 1.2].

Definition 2.3.

For a knot KK, define its augmentation rank, meridional rank, and bridge number as follows:

ar⁡(K)\displaystyle\operatorname{ar}(K) :=max{dimVϵ:ϵ:Cord(K)→𝕜,ϵ(μ)≠1},\displaystyle:=\max\{\operatorname{dim}V_{\epsilon}:\epsilon\colon\operatorname{Cord}(K)\to\Bbbk,\ \epsilon(\mu)\neq 1\},
mr⁡(K)\displaystyle\operatorname{mr}(K) :=min⁡{r:πK​ is generated by ​r​ meridians},\displaystyle:=\min\{r:\pi_{K}\text{ is generated by }r\text{ meridians}\},
b⁡(K)\displaystyle b(K) :=min⁡{r:K​ admits an ​r​-bridge presentation}.\displaystyle:=\min\{r:K\text{ admits an }r\text{-bridge presentation}\}.

Via the augmentation-sheaf correspondence, the augmentation rank can also be read as the maximum rank of the irreducible diagonalizable microlocal rank one representations of πK\pi_{K}. The two occurrences of the word rank should not be confused. Microlocal rank records the normal jump along the conormal, whereas the other rank is rank in the usual sense.

We immediately have the following inequalities.

Proposition 2.4.

For every knot KK,

ar⁡(K)≤mr⁡(K)≤b⁡(K).\operatorname{ar}(K)\leq\operatorname{mr}(K)\leq b(K).
Proof.

By construction (2.1), the maximal value of dimVϵ\dim V_{\epsilon} is no larger than the number of meridional generators. Hence it yields

mr⁡(K)≤b⁡(K).\operatorname{mr}(K)\leq b(K).

∎

Let (ρ,V)(\rho,V) be a diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation. Since the distinguished meridian and the preferred longitude commute in the knot group, we can choose a suitable basis such that their representing matrices have the form

2.2. The Whitehead pattern and the satellite group

Let Wh:=C∪P⊂S3\mathrm{Wh}:=C\cup P\subset S^{3} be the oriented Whitehead link in standard position, where CC is the axis component and PP is the pattern component. Removing a tubular neighborhood of CC gives the solid torus

𝒱:=S3∖𝒪​p​(C),\mathcal{V}:=S^{3}\setminus\mathcal{O}p(C),

and the pattern component becomes a pattern P⊂𝒱P\subset\mathcal{V}. The pattern has winding number zero. Equivalently, its two longitudinal runs travel once around 𝒱\mathcal{V} with opposite orientations. Our peripheral convention on the outer boundary is

mC=ℓ𝒱,ℓC=m𝒱,m_{C}=\ell_{\mathcal{V}},\qquad\ell_{C}=m_{\mathcal{V}},

where (mC,ℓC)(m_{C},\ell_{C}) is the peripheral pair of the deleted axis. This fixes the notation in the gluing formulas below.

Definition 2.6.

Let P⊂𝒱P\subset\mathcal{V} be the Whitehead pattern fixed above. The untwisted Whitehead double of KK is the knot

where ϕK\phi_{K} is the zero-framed embedding chosen above. Thus its restriction to the boundary identifies the peripheral curves by

(ϕK)∗​(m𝒱)=mK,(ϕK)∗​(ℓ𝒱)=ℓK,(\phi_{K})_{*}(m_{\mathcal{V}})=m_{K},\qquad(\phi_{K})_{*}(\ell_{\mathcal{V}})=\ell_{K},

with ℓK\ell_{K} the preferred longitude of KK. The clasp sign is determined by our fixed choice of PP.

Orient all braid strands downward and let σi\sigma_{i} denote a positive right-handed crossing. One convenient braid representative for the oriented Whitehead link is

BW:=σ1​σ2−1​σ1​σ2−1​σ1∈B3,B_{W}:=\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}^{-1}\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}^{-1}\sigma_{1}\in B_{3},

where the first strand closes to CC and the other two strands close to PP. The four crossings between CC and PP have signed sum zero. The unique self-crossing of PP accounts for the correction from the braid framing to the preferred zero framing.

EP:=𝒱∖𝒪​p​(P).E_{P}:=\mathcal{V}\setminus\mathcal{O}p(P).

and ⟨m𝒱,ℓ𝒱⟩≅ℤ2\langle m_{\mathcal{V}},\ell_{\mathcal{V}}\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}^{2}. The meridian of the satellite component is x1x_{1}.

Proposition 2.8.

Suppose KK is a non-trivial knot. The knot group of the Whitehead double can be computed by

2.3. The one-step doubling construction

A μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation of πWh⁡(K)\pi_{\operatorname{Wh}(K)} restricts to a representation of πK\pi_{K} of microlocal rank at most two. The goal of this subsection is to describe the reverse construction: starting with a μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation of πK\pi_{K}, we first pass to a representation of πK\pi_{K} of microlocal rank two and then extend it across the pattern exterior to obtain a μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation of πWh⁡(K)\pi_{\operatorname{Wh}(K)}.

We first record the algebraic construction used in the doubling argument. Let GG be a group and let ρ:G→GL⁡(V)\rho\colon G\to\operatorname{GL}(V) be a finite-dimensional representation. Put V∗:=Hom𝕜⁡(V,𝕜)V^{*}:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(V,\Bbbk). The dual representation (ρ∗,V∗)(\rho^{*},V^{*}) is defined by (ρ∗​(g)​φ)​(v):=φ⁡(ρ⁡(g−1)​v),g∈G,φ∈V∗,v∈V.\bigl(\rho^{*}(g)\varphi\bigr)(v):=\varphi\bigl(\rho(g^{-1})v\bigr),g\in G,\ \varphi\in V^{*},\ v\in V.

Let ρ:πK⟶GL⁡(V)\rho\colon\pi_{K}\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(V) be an nn-dimensional diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation. Theorem 2.12.

Let ρ:πK→GL⁡(V)\rho\colon\pi_{K}\to\operatorname{GL}(V) be an nn-dimensional irreducible diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation. Then the distinguished μ~\widetilde{\mu}-eigenvector of X~2\widetilde{X}_{2} is v2:=λ−1​e+λ​e∗v_{2}:=\lambda^{-1}e+\lambda e^{*}. Because λ2≠1\lambda^{2}\neq 1, we have

λ​ρ~​(g)​v1−ρ~​(g)​v2λ−λ−1=ρ⁡(g)​e⊕0,ρ~​(g)​v2−λ−1​ρ~​(g)​v1λ−λ−1=0⊕ρ∗​(g)​e∗.\frac{\lambda\widetilde{\rho}(g)v_{1}-\widetilde{\rho}(g)v_{2}}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}=\rho(g)e\oplus 0,\qquad\frac{\widetilde{\rho}(g)v_{2}-\lambda^{-1}\widetilde{\rho}(g)v_{1}}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}=0\oplus\rho^{*}(g)e^{*}.

Since w1​(v1)=μ~−1w_{1}(v_{1})=\widetilde{\mu}-1, we normalize it to v1∗:=w1/(μ~−1)v_{1}^{*}:=w_{1}/(\widetilde{\mu}-1), so as to pair with v1v_{1}. The preceding arguments imply

(2.10) Span⁡{ρ~​(h)​v1:h∈πWh⁡(K)}=V⊕V∗,Span⁡{ρ~∗​(h)​v1∗:h∈πWh⁡(K)}=(V⊕V∗)∗.\operatorname{Span}\{\widetilde{\rho}(h)v_{1}:h\in\pi_{\operatorname{Wh}(K)}\}=V\oplus V^{*},\qquad\operatorname{Span}\!\left\{\widetilde{\rho}^{*}(h)v_{1}^{*}:h\in\pi_{\operatorname{Wh}(K)}\right\}=(V\oplus V^{*})^{*}.

Corollary 2.13.

Let KK be a nontrivial knot admitting an nn-dimensional irreducible diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation whose peripheral data (μ,λ)(\mu,\lambda) satisfy (2.6) in Lemma 2.10. If n=b⁡(K)n=b(K), then

(2.11) Ri​j=(1−μ~)​(v1∗​ρ~​(gi))​(ρ~​(gj−1)​v1).R_{ij}=(1-\widetilde{\mu})\left(v_{1}^{*}\widetilde{\rho}(g_{i})\right)\bigl(\widetilde{\rho}(g_{j}^{-1})v_{1}\bigr).

The Whitehead pattern has geometric index two. A minimal bridge presentation of KK gives a doubled bridge presentation of Wh⁡(K)\operatorname{Wh}(K), while the satellite bridge inequality gives the reverse bound. Since KK is nontrivial, these two bounds apply and give

see [18, Section 4]. Proposition 2.4 now yields

2​n≤ar⁡(Wh⁡(K))≤mr⁡(Wh⁡(K))≤b⁡(Wh⁡(K))=2​n,2n\leq\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}(K))\leq\operatorname{mr}(\operatorname{Wh}(K))\leq b(\operatorname{Wh}(K))=2n,

and all three ranks are equal to 2​n2n. ∎

Proposition 2.14.

The peripheral data of ρ~:πWh⁡(K)→GL⁡(V⊕V∗)\widetilde{\rho}\colon\pi_{\operatorname{Wh}(K)}\to\operatorname{GL}(V\oplus V^{*}) are the following:

2.4. Iteration and the algebraic peripheral correspondence

The main conclusion of the preceding section is a rank-doubling construction. Starting from an nn-dimensional irreducible diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation of πK\pi_{K}, under suitable conditions, we obtain a 2​n2n-dimensional irreducible diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation of πWh⁡(K)\pi_{\operatorname{Wh}(K)}. If the construction can be repeated NN times, it produces a 2N​n2^{N}n-dimensional representation of πWhN⁡(K)\pi_{\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K)}, and hence ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))≥2N​n\operatorname{ar}\bigl(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K)\bigr)\geq 2^{N}n.

Most of the constructions work for any field 𝕜\Bbbk, but we eventually take 𝕜=ℂ\Bbbk=\mathbb{C} for the geometric application. An affine algebraic set is a common zero locus of polynomials, with its Zariski topology; it need not be irreducible. We write 𝕜⁡[A]\Bbbk[A] for its coordinate ring. A regular function on an open subset is locally a quotient of polynomials with a nonvanishing denominator. An algebraic set is irreducible if it is nonempty and not a union of two proper closed subsets. An irreducible component is a maximal irreducible closed subset. A nonempty open subset of an irreducible algebraic set is dense, and a morphism is dominant if its image is dense. Dimension is the maximum length of a strict chain of nonempty irreducible closed subsets. A zero-dimensional irreducible algebraic set is a point, and a curve is irreducible and one-dimensional. See [23, Chapter I, Sections 1–4].

A subset is constructible if it is a finite union of locally closed subsets. Chevalley’s theorem says that the image of a constructible set under a morphism is constructible [19, Chapter 1, Theorem 4.91 and Observation 4.92]. We shall also use the elementary consequence that a dense constructible subset of an irreducible algebraic set contains a nonempty open subset. These conventions apply to the peripheral tori and correspondences below.

Let (𝕜×)2(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2} be the algebraic torus with coordinates (μ,η=λ2)(\mu,\eta=\lambda^{2}). Recall from Section 2.3 that the Whitehead doubling construction requires (μ,η)∈𝒰(\mu,\eta)\in\mathcal{U}, where

𝒰:={(μ,η)∈(𝕜×)2:(μ−1)​(η−1)​(μ​η+1)​(μ2​η2−μ​η2+4​μ​η−μ+1)≠0}.\mathcal{U}:=\left\{(\mu,\eta)\in(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2}:(\mu-1)(\eta-1)(\mu\eta+1)(\mu^{2}\eta^{2}-\mu\eta^{2}+4\mu\eta-\mu+1)\neq 0\right\}.

Here the first constraint is to ensure that ρ⁡(mK)\rho(m_{K}) is diagonalizable, and the remaining three constraints are the hypotheses (2.6) used in Lemma 2.10, Theorem 2.12 and Corollary 2.13, with reasons explained in Remark 2.11. As we repeat the doubling construction, the same conditions must hold for the output peripheral data at every stage. We begin with the definition for the loci where NN iterations are allowed.

Definition 2.15.

Define a length-NN sequence consisting of

((μj,ηj)0≤j≤N,(aj,dj)0≤j<N)∈(𝕜×)2​N+2×𝕜2​N,\big((\mu_{j},\eta_{j})_{0\leq j\leq N},(a_{j},d_{j})_{0\leq j<N}\big)\in(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2N+2}\times\Bbbk^{2N},

satisfying the following conditions:

  1. (1)

    doubling constraints: for 0≤j<N0\leq j<N,

    μj≠1,ηj≠1,ηj​μj≠−1,ηj2​μj2−ηj2​μj+4​ηj​μj−μj+1≠0;\mu_{j}\neq 1,\qquad\eta_{j}\neq 1,\qquad\eta_{j}\mu_{j}\neq-1,\qquad\eta_{j}^{2}\mu_{j}^{2}-\eta_{j}^{2}\mu_{j}+4\eta_{j}\mu_{j}-\mu_{j}+1\neq 0;
  2. (2)

    internal relations: for 0≤j<N0\leq j<N,

    aj=μj​dj,ηj​(1−μj)​aj​dj+(μj​ηj2−1)​(aj−1)​(dj−1)=0.a_{j}=\mu_{j}d_{j},\qquad\eta_{j}(1-\mu_{j})a_{j}d_{j}+(\mu_{j}\eta_{j}^{2}-1)(a_{j}-1)(d_{j}-1)=0.
  3. (3)

    inductive relations: for 0≤j<N0\leq j<N,

    μj+1:=aj+dj−1,ηj+1:=(ηj​(aj−1)+(dj−1)(aj−1)+ηj​(dj−1))2.\mu_{j+1}:=a_{j}+d_{j}-1,\qquad\eta_{j+1}:=\left(\frac{\eta_{j}(a_{j}-1)+(d_{j}-1)}{(a_{j}-1)+\eta_{j}(d_{j}-1)}\right)^{2}.

Let 𝒞N\mathcal{C}_{N} be the set of length-NN sequences. Define the projection

pr:(𝕜×)2​N+2×𝕜2​N\displaystyle\operatorname{pr}:\quad(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2N+2}\times\Bbbk^{2N} ⟶(𝕜×)2,\displaystyle\longrightarrow(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2},
((μj,ηj),(aj,dj))\displaystyle\left((\mu_{j},\eta_{j}),(a_{j},d_{j})\right) ⟼(μ0,η0).\displaystyle\longmapsto(\mu_{0},\eta_{0}).

Define 𝒮N:=pr⁡(𝒞N)\mathcal{S}_{N}:=\operatorname{pr}(\mathcal{C}_{N}) to be the image. Note that 𝒮0=(𝕜×)2\mathcal{S}_{0}=(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2} and 𝒮1=𝒰\mathcal{S}_{1}=\mathcal{U}. Moreover, by truncating a length-(N+1)(N+1) sequence, we have

𝒮N+1⊆𝒮N.\mathcal{S}_{N+1}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{N}.

A length-NN sequence records the compatible data required to carry out NN successive doubling steps. Suitable initial peripheral data would start the iteration.

Proposition 2.16.

Let ρ0:πK→GL⁡(V0)\rho_{0}\colon\pi_{K}\to\operatorname{GL}(V_{0}) be an nn-dimensional irreducible diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation with peripheral data (μ0,λ0)(\mu_{0},\lambda_{0}). Suppose (μ0,λ02)∈𝒮N(\mu_{0},\lambda_{0}^{2})\in\mathcal{S}_{N}. Then for each 0≤j≤N0\leq j\leq N, there exists a 2j​n2^{j}n-dimensional irreducible diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation ρj:πWhj⁡(K)⟶GL⁡(Vj)\rho_{j}\colon\pi_{\operatorname{Wh}^{j}(K)}\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(V_{j}).

Proof.

Choose a length-NN sequence ((μj,ηj)0≤j≤N,(aj,dj)0≤j<N)\big((\mu_{j},\eta_{j})_{0\leq j\leq N},(a_{j},d_{j})_{0\leq j<N}\big) representing (μ0,λ02)∈𝒮N(\mu_{0},\lambda_{0}^{2})\in\mathcal{S}_{N}. The doubling constraints allow the construction at every stage, while the inductive relations and the peripheral formula give μj+1=aj+dj−1\mu_{j+1}=a_{j}+d_{j}-1 and λj+12=ηj+1\lambda_{j+1}^{2}=\eta_{j+1}. Induction therefore gives irreducible diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representations

ρj:πWhj⁡(K)⟶GL⁡(Vj),0≤j≤N.\rho_{j}\colon\pi_{\operatorname{Wh}^{j}(K)}\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(V_{j}),\qquad 0\leq j\leq N.

Since dimVj+1=2​dimVj\dim V_{j+1}=2\dim V_{j}, we have dimVj=2j​n\dim V_{j}=2^{j}n. ∎

Corollary 2.17.

Let KK be nontrivial, and let ρ0:πK→GL⁡(V0)\rho_{0}\colon\pi_{K}\to\operatorname{GL}(V_{0}) be an nn-dimensional irreducible diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation with peripheral data (μ0,λ0)(\mu_{0},\lambda_{0}). If b⁡(K)=nb(K)=n and (μ0,λ02)∈𝒮N(\mu_{0},\lambda_{0}^{2})\in\mathcal{S}_{N}, then

(2.15) ar⁡(Whj⁡(K))=mr⁡(Whj⁡(K))=b⁡(Whj⁡(K))=2j​n,0≤j≤N.\operatorname{ar}\bigl(\operatorname{Wh}^{j}(K)\bigr)=\operatorname{mr}\bigl(\operatorname{Wh}^{j}(K)\bigr)=b\bigl(\operatorname{Wh}^{j}(K)\bigr)=2^{j}n,\qquad 0\leq j\leq N.
Proof.

This proof iterates the argument in Corollary 2.13 NN times. Namely, Proposition 2.16 yields ar⁡(Whj⁡(K))≥2j​n.\operatorname{ar}\bigl(\operatorname{Wh}^{j}(K)\bigr)\geq 2^{j}n. Iterating the doubled bridge presentation gives b⁡(Whj⁡(K))≤2j​b​(K)=2j​n.b\bigl(\operatorname{Wh}^{j}(K)\bigr)\leq 2^{j}b(K)=2^{j}n. Together with Proposition 2.4, these bounds give

2j​n≤ar⁡(Whj⁡(K))≤mr⁡(Whj⁡(K))≤b⁡(Whj⁡(K))≤2j​n,2^{j}n\leq\operatorname{ar}\bigl(\operatorname{Wh}^{j}(K)\bigr)\leq\operatorname{mr}\bigl(\operatorname{Wh}^{j}(K)\bigr)\leq b\bigl(\operatorname{Wh}^{j}(K)\bigr)\leq 2^{j}n,

which proves the claimed equalities. ∎

Example 2.18.

We now consider the case when K=31K=3_{1} is the right-handed trefoil, which has bridge index 22. A routine computation shows that we can express its knot group as

πK=⟨a,b|aba=bab⟩.\pi_{K}=\langle a,b~|~aba=bab\rangle.

Furthermore, we can identify mK=am_{K}=a and ℓK=(a​b)3​a−6\ell_{K}=(ab)^{3}a^{-6}. We can write down a concrete representation

ρ:πK→GL⁡(ℂ2)\rho:\pi_{K}\to{\rm GL}(\mathbb{C}^{2})

as

ρ⁡(a)=(2101)​and​ρ​(b)=(10−22)\rho(a)=\left(\begin{matrix}2&1\\ 0&1\end{matrix}\right)\ \text{and}\ \rho(b)=\left(\begin{matrix}1&0\\ -2&2\end{matrix}\right)

One can verify it is indeed a diagonalizable μ​rk\mu{\rm rk}-one representation with peripheral data (μ0,λ0)=(2,−18)(\mu_{0},\lambda_{0})=(2,-\frac{1}{8}). At each iteration, there are two choices of μ\mu, which are roots of the quadratic polynomial in (2.9). Since the two distinct candidates are inverse to each other, we always take the one whose norm is greater than 11. This provides an iteration (μn,λn2)→(μn+1,λn+12)(\mu_{n},\lambda_{n}^{2})\to(\mu_{n+1},\lambda_{n+1}^{2}) provided (μn,λn2)∈𝒮1(\mu_{n},\lambda_{n}^{2})\in\mathcal{S}_{1}. A short Python script prints the peripheral data of the first five iterations as follows.

With some effort, one could show that the initial data (2,164)(2,\frac{1}{64}) lies in 𝒮N\mathcal{S}_{N} for all NN. The final remark is to note that this infinite iteration stays “bounded” in contrast to the iterable branches discussed in Section 4.1.

Note that the above discussion does not involve the consideration of a specific knot KK. The sets 𝒮N\mathcal{S}_{N} depend only on the Whitehead pattern, not on the companion knot. To apply the construction to a given companion KK for a prescribed number NN of steps, one must find a representation of the required dimension whose peripheral data satisfy (μ,λ2)∈𝒮N(\mu,\lambda^{2})\in\mathcal{S}_{N}. We next show that each 𝒮N\mathcal{S}_{N} contains a Zariski-open dense subset of the ambient peripheral torus. This statement does not by itself imply that 𝒮N\mathcal{S}_{N} meets a prescribed peripheral curve of KK. The next proposition shows an essential property of 𝒮N\mathcal{S}_{N}, which asserts enough general points.

Proposition 2.19.

For every N≥0N\geq 0, the set 𝒮N\mathcal{S}_{N} is constructible and contains a Zariski-open dense subset of (𝕜×)2(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2}. Moreover, since 𝕜=ℂ\Bbbk=\mathbb{C} is uncountable, ∩N∈ℕ𝒮N\cap_{N\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{S}_{N} is Zariski dense.

To prove this proposition, we first consider the correspondence defined by the doubling construction. Consider two tori (𝕜×)(μ,η)2(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2}_{({\mu},{\eta})} and (𝕜×)(μ~,λ~)2(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2}_{(\widetilde{\mu},\widetilde{\lambda})}. Let π1,π2\pi_{1},\pi_{2} be the projections from the product to the first and second components. We also define π~2{\widetilde{\pi}_{2}} by

π~2​(μ,η,μ~,λ~):=(μ~,λ~2){\widetilde{\pi}_{2}}(\mu,\eta,\widetilde{\mu},\widetilde{\lambda}):=(\widetilde{\mu},\widetilde{\lambda}^{2})

These maps fit into the commutative diagram

We formulate a correspondence between (μ,η)(\mu,\eta) and (μ~,λ~)(\widetilde{\mu},\widetilde{\lambda}) from the iteration procedure. Recall from (2.9) that μ~\widetilde{\mu} is the solution of Pη,μ​(μ~)=0P_{\eta,\mu}(\widetilde{\mu})=0, and from (2.12) that λ\lambda is a rational polynomial. Let δ⁡(μ,η,μ~):=μ​η−μ​μ~−η​μ~+1\delta(\mu,\eta,\widetilde{\mu}):=\mu\eta-\mu\widetilde{\mu}-\eta\widetilde{\mu}+1 be the denominator, then we can rewrite the expression as a polynomial δ​λ~+μ​η​μ~−μ−η+μ~=0\delta\widetilde{\lambda}+\mu\eta\widetilde{\mu}-\mu-\eta+\widetilde{\mu}=0. Then we define:

(2.16) 𝒲^:={(μ,η,μ~,λ~):Pη,μ(μ~)=0,δλ~+μημ~−μ−η+μ~=0}⊂(𝕜×)(μ,η)2×(𝕜×)(μ~,λ~)2.\widehat{\mathcal{W}}:=\left\{(\mu,\eta,\widetilde{\mu},\widetilde{\lambda}):P_{\eta,\mu}(\widetilde{\mu})=0,\,\delta\widetilde{\lambda}+\mu\eta\widetilde{\mu}-\mu-\eta+\widetilde{\mu}=0\right\}\subset(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2}_{(\mu,\eta)}\times(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2}_{(\widetilde{\mu},\widetilde{\lambda})}.

Note that Pη,μ​(μ~)=0P_{\eta,\mu}(\widetilde{\mu})=0 is generically quadratic, namely

Pη,μ​(μ~)=A​μ~2+B​μ~+A,P_{\eta,\mu}(\widetilde{\mu})=A\widetilde{\mu}^{2}+B\widetilde{\mu}+A,

where

A\displaystyle A =μ​(η−1)​(η​μ+1),\displaystyle=\mu(\eta-1)(\eta\mu+1),
B\displaystyle B =1+μ2+2​η​μ−2​η​μ2−η2​μ−η2​μ3.\displaystyle=1+\mu^{2}+2\eta\mu-2\eta\mu^{2}-\eta^{2}\mu-\eta^{2}\mu^{3}.

The discriminant is

(2.17) B2−4​A2=(μ−1)​(μ+1)2​(μ​η2−1)​(μ2​η2−μ​η2+4​μ​η−μ+1).B^{2}-4A^{2}=(\mu-1)(\mu+1)^{2}(\mu\eta^{2}-1)(\mu^{2}\eta^{2}-\mu\eta^{2}+4\mu\eta-\mu+1).

Under the conditions μ≠−1\mu\neq-1 and μ​η2≠1\mu\eta^{2}\neq 1, the discriminant is non-zero. Hence, we introduce the Zariski-open subset

𝒰′:={(μ,η)∈𝒰:μ≠−1,μη2≠1}⊂𝒰⊂(𝕜×)(μ,η)2.\mathcal{U}^{\prime}:=\bigl\{(\mu,\eta)\in\mathcal{U}:\mu\neq-1,\,\mu\eta^{2}\neq 1\bigr\}\subset\mathcal{U}\subset(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2}_{(\mu,\eta)}.

Finally, we introduce

𝒲:=Closure​(𝒲^∩π1−1​(𝒰′))∩𝒲^.\mathcal{W}:=\text{Closure}(\widehat{\mathcal{W}}\cap\pi_{1}^{-1}(\mathcal{U}^{\prime}))\cap\widehat{\mathcal{W}}.

This is the correspondence that we will work with.

Proposition 2.20.

We have the following properties:

  1. (1)

    𝒲\mathcal{W} is irreducible.

  2. (2)

    π1|𝒲:𝒲→(𝕜×)(μ,η)2\pi_{1}|_{\mathcal{W}}:\mathcal{W}\rightarrow(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2}_{(\mu,\eta)} is dominant and generically two-to-one.

  3. (3)

    π2|𝒲:𝒲→(𝕜×)(μ~,λ~)2\pi_{2}|_{\mathcal{W}}:\mathcal{W}\to(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2}_{(\widetilde{\mu},\widetilde{\lambda})} is dominant and generically at most two-to-one.

  4. (4)

    π~2|𝒲:𝒲→(𝕜×)(μ~,η~)2\widetilde{\pi}_{2}|_{\mathcal{W}}:\mathcal{W}\to(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2}_{(\widetilde{\mu},\widetilde{\eta})} is also dominant.

Proof.

(1) Over the Zariski-open dense subset 𝒰′\mathcal{U}^{\prime}, Pη,μ​(μ~)=0P_{\eta,\mu}(\widetilde{\mu})=0 has two distinct solutions. Moreover, the discriminant B2−4​A2B^{2}-4A^{2} is not a square in 𝕜⁡(μ,η)\Bbbk(\mu,\eta), and Pη,μP_{\eta,\mu} is irreducible over 𝕜⁡(μ,η)\Bbbk(\mu,\eta). Indeed, to see the non-squareness, the factor (μ−1)(\mu-1) has order 1. The other factors (μ+1)(\mu+1), (μ​η2−1)(\mu\eta^{2}-1), (μ2​η2−μ​η2+4​μ​η−μ+1)(\mu^{2}\eta^{2}-\mu\eta^{2}+4\mu\eta-\mu+1) do not contain any power of (μ−1)(\mu-1), because when evaluated at μ=1\mu=1, they equal 2,(η2−1),4​η2,(\eta^{2}-1),4\eta respectively, none of which is zero.

The coefficients of Pη,μ​(μ~)P_{\eta,\mu}(\widetilde{\mu}) have no common factors, making it primitive. By Gauss’s lemma, Pη,μ​(μ~)P_{\eta,\mu}(\widetilde{\mu}) is also irreducible over 𝕜⁡[μ,η]\Bbbk[\mu,\eta]. Once η,μ,μ~\eta,\mu,\widetilde{\mu} are fixed, λ~\widetilde{\lambda} is uniquely determined as a rational polynomial. In particular, over the Zariski-open dense locus δ≠0{\delta\neq 0}, the variety is irreducible. The exceptional case, since we transformed the equation of λ~\widetilde{\lambda} into a polynomial, is that both the numerator and denominator equal zero, i.e. μ​η​μ~−μ−η+μ~=0,μ​η−μ​μ~−η​μ~+1=0.\mu\eta\widetilde{\mu}-\mu-\eta+\widetilde{\mu}=0,\mu\eta-\mu\widetilde{\mu}-\eta\widetilde{\mu}+1=0. (2) Since 𝒰′\mathcal{U}^{\prime} is open dense in (𝕜×)(μ,η)2(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2}_{(\mu,\eta)}, π1|𝒲\pi_{1}|_{\mathcal{W}} is dominant. A generic fiber has two choices of μ~\widetilde{\mu} and a corresponding λ~\widetilde{\lambda}.

We next identify the part of the correspondence on which the one-step construction is nondegenerate. Define

(2.18) 𝒲step:={w=(μ,η,μ~,λ~)∈𝒲:π1(w)∈𝒰,δ(μ,η,μ~)≠0}.\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{step}}:=\left\{w=(\mu,\eta,\widetilde{\mu},\widetilde{\lambda})\in\mathcal{W}:\pi_{1}(w)\in\mathcal{U},\ \delta(\mu,\eta,\widetilde{\mu})\neq 0\right\}.

μ~=a+d−1,λ~=η⁡(a−1)+(d−1)(a−1)+η⁡(d−1),\widetilde{\mu}=a+d-1,\qquad\widetilde{\lambda}=\frac{\eta(a-1)+(d-1)}{(a-1)+\eta(d-1)},

a=μ⁡(μ~+1)μ+1d=μ~+1μ+1.a=\frac{\mu(\widetilde{\mu}+1)}{\mu+1}\qquad d=\frac{\widetilde{\mu}+1}{\mu+1}.

𝒢0:=(𝕜×)2,𝒢N+1:=π1​(𝒲step∩π~2−1​(𝒢N)).\mathcal{G}_{0}:=(\Bbbk^{\times})^{2},\qquad\mathcal{G}_{N+1}:=\pi_{1}\!\left(\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{step}}\cap\widetilde{\pi}_{2}^{-1}(\mathcal{G}_{N})\right).

(2.19) 𝒢N⊆𝒮N.\mathcal{G}_{N}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{N}.

Proof.

Proof of Proposition 2.19.

Following Definition 2.15, 𝒞N\mathcal{C}_{N} is defined by a finite collection of polynomials and non-vanishing conditions, hence it is locally closed and further constructible. Iterate the argument for the second variable, we find η0\eta_{0} such that neither g⁡(μ0,η0)g(\mu_{0},\eta_{0}) nor any fN​(μ0,η0)f_{N}(\mu_{0},\eta_{0}) vanished. This completes the proof. ∎

2.5. Meridional bounds

We next compare the representations constructed in Section 2.4 with meridional generating sets. The upper bound below does not require an augmentation or a condition on its peripheral data.

Proposition 2.22.

For every knot KK and every integer N≥0N\geq 0,

mr⁡(Wh⁡(K))≤2​mr⁡(K),mr⁡(WhN⁡(K))≤2N​mr⁡(K).\operatorname{mr}(\operatorname{Wh}(K))\leq 2\operatorname{mr}(K),\qquad\operatorname{mr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\leq 2^{N}\operatorname{mr}(K).
Proof.

Let r=mr⁡(K)r=\operatorname{mr}(K). Choose meridional generators mi=hi​mK​hi−1m_{i}=h_{i}m_{K}h_{i}^{-1}, 1≤i≤r1\leq i\leq r, with h1=1h_{1}=1. In the satellite presentation of Proposition 2.8, we have

m𝒱=x2​x1−1​x2−1​x1=mK,ℓ𝒱=ℓK,ℓ𝒱​x2​ℓ𝒱−1=x1.m_{\mathcal{V}}=x_{2}x_{1}^{-1}x_{2}^{-1}x_{1}=m_{K},\qquad\ell_{\mathcal{V}}=\ell_{K},\qquad\ell_{\mathcal{V}}x_{2}\ell_{\mathcal{V}}^{-1}=x_{1}.

In particular, both x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} are meridians of Wh⁡(K)\operatorname{Wh}(K). Let HH be the subgroup generated by the 2​r2r meridians

ui=hi​x1​hi−1,vi=hi​x2​hi−1,1≤i≤r.u_{i}=h_{i}x_{1}h_{i}^{-1},\qquad v_{i}=h_{i}x_{2}h_{i}^{-1},\qquad 1\leq i\leq r.

Here elements of the companion group are understood through their images in the satellite group. For each ii,

vi​ui−1​vi−1​ui=hi​(x2​x1−1​x2−1​x1)​hi−1=mi.v_{i}u_{i}^{-1}v_{i}^{-1}u_{i}=h_{i}(x_{2}x_{1}^{-1}x_{2}^{-1}x_{1})h_{i}^{-1}=m_{i}.

Thus HH contains the image of the companion group, and hence ℓ𝒱\ell_{\mathcal{V}}. It also contains x1=u1x_{1}=u_{1} and x2=v1x_{2}=v_{1}. These elements generate the pattern group. The satellite presentation therefore gives H=πWh⁡(K)H=\pi_{\operatorname{Wh}(K)}, proving the first inequality. Induction gives the second. The same presentation argument applies when KK is the unknot; it does not require the companion homomorphism to be injective. ∎

Together with Proposition 2.4, this gives the unconditional bounds

(2.20) ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))≤mr⁡(WhN⁡(K))≤2N​mr⁡(K).\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\leq\operatorname{mr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\leq 2^{N}\operatorname{mr}(K).

The next result gives a sufficient condition for equality. Recall the chain-admitting set 𝒮N\mathcal{S}_{N} from Definition 2.15 and the paragraph following it.

Theorem 2.23.

Let KK be a knot and set r=mr⁡(K)r=\operatorname{mr}(K). Suppose that KK admits a rank-rr augmentation ϵ\epsilon with ϵ⁡(μ)≠1\epsilon(\mu)\neq 1 and

(ϵ⁡(μ),ϵ​(λ)2)∈𝒮N.\bigl(\epsilon(\mu),\epsilon(\lambda)^{2}\bigr)\in\mathcal{S}_{N}.

Then

ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))=mr⁡(WhN⁡(K))=2N​mr⁡(K).\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=\operatorname{mr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=2^{N}\operatorname{mr}(K).
Proof.

The augmentation–representation correspondence recalled in Section 2.1 gives an irreducible rr-dimensional diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation with the prescribed peripheral data. Proposition 2.16 then gives ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))≥2N​r\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\geq 2^{N}r. Combining this with (2.20) proves the result. ∎

Remark 2.24.

The condition on the peripheral point is essential. In Section 6, we show that the square knot SS satisfies ar⁡(S)=mr⁡(S)=b⁡(S)=3\operatorname{ar}(S)=\operatorname{mr}(S)=b(S)=3, whereas ar⁡(Wh⁡(S))≤5\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}(S))\leq 5. Thus maximal augmentation rank for the companion alone does not suffice.

3. Algebraic curves and character varieties

Theorem 2.23 reduces the meridional-rank problem to finding an augmentation whose peripheral point lies in 𝒮N\mathcal{S}_{N}. To make this choice for every NN, we use a curve of peripheral values. We first recall how a point at infinity of such a curve determines the orders of poles and zeros. We then record the character-variety constructions used to obtain the curve from a boundary slope. Throughout this section, the ground field is ℂ\mathbb{C}, and we use the algebraic conventions of Section 2.4.

3.1. Curves, ideal points, and valuations

For an irreducible algebraic set AA, we denote its field of rational functions by ℂ⁡(A)\mathbb{C}(A). A rational map is defined on a nonempty open subset, not necessarily on its whole source; two representatives define the same map if they agree on their common domain. A birational map restricts to an isomorphism between nonempty open subsets. We write Dom⁡(φ)\operatorname{Dom}(\varphi) for the largest open subset on which a rational map φ\varphi is defined.

Definition 3.1.

Suppose CC is an affine algebraic curve. A smooth projective model (C~,ϕ~)(\widetilde{C},\tilde{\phi}) of CC is a smooth projective curve C~\widetilde{C} together with a birational map ϕ~:C~⇢C\tilde{\phi}:\widetilde{C}\dashrightarrow C. A point P∈C~P\in\widetilde{C} not in the domain of ϕ~\tilde{\phi} is called an ideal point of CC.

Every affine algebraic curve has a smooth projective model [23, Chapter I, Corollary 6.11]. The birational map identifies ℂ⁡(C)\mathbb{C}(C) with ℂ⁡(C~)\mathbb{C}(\widetilde{C}); we use this identification for rational functions throughout. The following lemma is important to lift valuation-related results from the PSL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) setup to the SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) setup.

Lemma 3.2.

Suppose f:C→Df:C\to D is a morphism between two affine algebraic curves so that D=im⁡(f)¯D=\overline{\operatorname{im}(f)}. Suppose (C~,ϕ~C)(\widetilde{C},\tilde{\phi}_{C}) and (D~,ϕ~D)(\widetilde{D},\tilde{\phi}_{D}) are the respective smooth projective models. Then there exists a unique surjective morphism f~:C~→D~\tilde{f}:\widetilde{C}\to\widetilde{D} such that as rational maps we have ϕ~D∘f~=f∘ϕ~C.\tilde{\phi}_{D}\circ\tilde{f}=f\circ\tilde{\phi}_{C}.

Proof.

The existence of a dominant morphism f~:C~→D~\tilde{f}:\widetilde{C}\to\widetilde{D} with the identity ϕ~D∘f~=f∘ϕ~C\tilde{\phi}_{D}\circ\tilde{f}=f\circ\tilde{\phi}_{C} is established in [23, Chapter I, Corollary 6.12]. The meaning of “dominant” is precisely what we assumed (D=im⁡(f)¯D=\overline{\operatorname{im}(f)}). [19, Chapter 1, Theorem 4.100] says that C~\widetilde{C} is complete, and hence by [19, Chapter 1, Theorem 4.98] the image of f~\tilde{f} is closed, and must be all of D~\widetilde{D}. ∎

Let P∈C~P\in\widetilde{C}. Denote by 𝒪C~,P\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{C},P} the local ring of rational functions regular near PP, and by 𝔪C~,P\mathfrak{m}_{\widetilde{C},P} its maximal ideal of functions vanishing at PP. Since C~\widetilde{C} is a smooth curve, this local ring is a discrete valuation ring [23, Chapter I, Theorems 5.1 and 6.2A]. In particular, 𝔪C~,P\mathfrak{m}_{\widetilde{C},P} has a generator ss, and every nonzero f∈ℂ⁡(C~)f\in\mathbb{C}(\widetilde{C}) has a unique expression f=sk​hf=s^{k}h with k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z} and hh a unit in 𝒪C~,P\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{C},P}. The integer kk is independent of the choice of ss.

Definition 3.3.

A generator ss of 𝔪C~,P\mathfrak{m}_{\widetilde{C},P} is a local parameter at PP. For f=sk​hf=s^{k}h as above, its valuation at PP is νP​(f)=k\nu_{P}(f)=k, and its pole order is

poleP⁡(f)=max⁡{0,−νP​(f)}.\operatorname{pole}_{P}(f)=\max\{0,-\nu_{P}(f)\}.

We set νP​(0)=+∞\nu_{P}(0)=+\infty. Thus zeros have positive valuation and poles have negative valuation.

The next lemma explains why the inequalities between valuations used later are preserved when we pass to a covering curve.

Lemma 3.4.

Suppose ψ:C~→C~′\psi:\widetilde{C}\to\widetilde{C}^{\prime} is a surjective morphism between two smooth projective curves. Let P∈C~P\in\widetilde{C} and Q=ψ⁡(P)Q=\psi(P). Let sQs_{Q} be the local parameter at QQ as in Definition 3.3. Write

e⁡(P/Q)=νP​(ψ∗​(sQ)).e(P/Q)=\nu_{P}(\psi^{*}(s_{Q})).

Then the following statements are true:

  • •

    The value e⁡(P/Q)e(P/Q) is a positive integer and independent of the choice of the local parameter sQs_{Q}.

  • •

    For any nonzero rational function ff on C~′\widetilde{C}^{\prime}, we have

    νP​(ψ∗​f)=e⁡(P/Q)​νQ​(f).\nu_{P}(\psi^{*}f)=e(P/Q)\nu_{Q}(f).

    Consequently, we have

    poleP⁡(ψ∗​f)=e⁡(P/Q)​poleQ⁡(f).\operatorname{pole}_{P}(\psi^{*}f)=e(P/Q)\operatorname{pole}_{Q}(f).
Proof.

Since by construction sQ​(Q)=0s_{Q}(Q)=0, we have (ψ∗​sQ)​(P)=0(\psi^{*}s_{Q})(P)=0. [23, Chapter I, Theorem 4.4] implies that ψ∗​sQ\psi^{*}s_{Q} is not identically 00, and hence e⁡(P/Q)=νP​(ψ∗​(sQ))e(P/Q)=\nu_{P}(\psi^{*}(s_{Q})) is a positive integer. It is clearly independent of the choice of sQs_{Q}: two different choices differ by the multiplication of a function nonzero at QQ whose pullback is nonzero at PP, so the valuation does not change. For any nonzero rational function ff, write f=sQk⋅uf=s_{Q}^{k}\cdot u. Then we have

ψ∗​(f)=(ψ∗​sQ)k⋅(ψ∗​u).\psi^{*}(f)=(\psi^{*}s_{Q})^{k}\cdot(\psi^{*}u).

The former has valuation k⋅e⁡(P/Q)k\cdot e(P/Q) and the latter is nonzero at PP. Hence we are done. ∎

We also need the analytic interpretation of a local parameter. The convergence in the following statement is used in Section 4.1.

Lemma 3.5 ([33, Chapter 2, Sections 2.1–2.3] and [34, Chapter 8, Section 1.1]).

Let C~\widetilde{C} be a smooth projective curve over ℂ\mathbb{C}, let P∈C~P\in\widetilde{C}, and let ss be a local parameter at PP. In the complex topology, there are a neighborhood VV of PP and ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that

s|V:V⟶Dε:={z∈ℂ:|z|<ε}s|_{V}:V\longrightarrow D_{\varepsilon}:=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<\varepsilon\}

is biholomorphic and sends PP to 00. We may take VV inside a Zariski-open neighborhood on which ss is regular. For every nonzero f∈ℂ⁡(C~)f\in\mathbb{C}(\widetilde{C}), after possibly shrinking this disc,

f∘(s|V)−1​(z)=∑j=k∞cj​zj,k=νP​(f),ck≠0,f\circ(s|_{V})^{-1}(z)=\sum_{j=k}^{\infty}c_{j}z^{j},\qquad k=\nu_{P}(f),\quad c_{k}\neq 0,

where the series converges on the punctured disc. The amount of shrinking may depend on ff.

Indeed, smooth complex algebraic curves are locally complex manifolds, and algebraic local parameters give analytic coordinates, as explained in [33, Chapter 2, Section 2.3]. Regular functions are holomorphic in these coordinates. Writing f=sk​hf=s^{k}h and expanding the holomorphic unit hh gives the asserted Laurent expansion. For any fixed finite collection of rational functions, one disc may be chosen for all of them by shrinking it once.

Let PP now be an ideal point of CC on its smooth projective model. The birational map ϕ~\tilde{\phi} is regular and injective on a nonempty Zariski-open subset of C~\widetilde{C}, whose complement is finite [33, Chapter I, Example 1.32 and Theorem 1.19]. We can therefore choose VV above so that ϕ~\tilde{\phi} is regular and injective on V∖{P}V\setminus\{P\}.

Definition 3.6.

Suppose CC is an affine algebraic curve, and (C~,ϕ~)(\widetilde{C},\tilde{\phi}) is its smooth projective model. A Puiseux branch is the choice of an ideal point P∈C~P\in\widetilde{C} and a local parameter ss at PP, together with suitable VV and ε\varepsilon supplied by the above lemma such that VV contains only one ideal point, namely PP, and ϕ~\tilde{\phi} is injective on V\{P}V\backslash\{P\}. Then we obtain the Puiseux parametrization

ϕ~∘(s|V\{P})−1:Dε\{0}→C.\tilde{\phi}\circ(s|_{V\backslash\{P\}})^{-1}:D_{\varepsilon}\backslash\{0\}\to C.

Through s|V:V→Dεs|_{V}:V\to D_{\varepsilon}, we may treat ss as the coordinate on DεD_{\varepsilon}. We treat the restriction

ϕ~∘(s|V\{P})−1|Dε′\{0}:Dε′\{0}→C\tilde{\phi}\circ(s|_{V\backslash\{P\}})^{-1}|_{D_{\varepsilon^{\prime}}\backslash\{0\}}:D_{\varepsilon^{\prime}}\backslash\{0\}\to C

for 0<ε′<ε0<\varepsilon^{\prime}<\varepsilon as the same Puiseux parametrization as the original.

This parametrization is injective and holomorphic. In an affine embedding of CC, its coordinate functions have the convergent Laurent expansions of Lemma 3.5. A proper closed subset of an irreducible curve is finite. An infinite subset is therefore dense. If it is constructible, it contains a nonempty open subset by the fact recalled in Section 2.4. We use this fact to pass from branches to open subsets in Section 4.1.

3.2. Character varieties and peripheral trace functions

For a knot K⊂S3K\subset S^{3}, define

RSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)=Hom⁡(πK,SL2⁡(ℂ)).R_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)=\operatorname{Hom}(\pi_{K},\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})).

A finite presentation of πK\pi_{K} realizes this as an affine algebraic set: the matrices assigned to the generators satisfy the determinant-one conditions and the equations given by the relators. Inversion is polynomial on SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}).

Definition 3.7.

The character of ρ∈RSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)\rho\in R_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) is the function χρ​(g)=tr⁡(ρ⁡(g))\chi_{\rho}(g)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(g)) on πK\pi_{K}. For g∈πKg\in\pi_{K}, the associated trace function is tg​(ρ)=tr⁡(ρ⁡(g))t_{g}(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(g)) on the representation set. We denote by TSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)T_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) the subalgebra of ℂ​[RSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]\mathbb{C}[R_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)] generated by these functions.

Note it is straightforward to check that all tgt_{g} are regular functions. We now construct the character variety XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) of KK. Observe that the group SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) acts on RSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)R_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) by conjugation: for an element h∈SL2⁡(ℂ)h\in\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) and ρ∈RSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)\rho\in R_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K), define

(h⋅ρ)​(g)=h⋅ρ⁡(g)⋅h−1,∀g∈πK(h\cdot\rho)(g)=h\cdot\rho(g)\cdot h^{-1},~\forall g\in\pi_{K}

Since SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) is reductive22 2 We refer the readers to [25] for the definition of reductivity and the fact that SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) is reductive. This definition is different from the one in [13, Definition 1.20], which we used to show the GIT quotient map is surjective, but the equivalence follows from [13, Definition 1.21 and Theorem 1.23]., it follows from [13, Theorem 1.24]33 3 The fact that the adjoint action is regular, which is needed as a hypothesis of the cited theorem, is straightforward to verify. that ℂ​[RSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]SL2⁡(ℂ)\mathbb{C}[R_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]^{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})} is finitely generated and defines an affine quotient with a surjective regular quotient map.

Definition 3.8.

The SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) character variety of KK is the affine quotient

XSL2⁡(ℂ)(K)=RSL2⁡(ℂ)(K)//SL2(ℂ).X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)=R_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)//\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}).

Its quotient map τ\tau identifies its coordinate ring with the invariant ring:

τ∗:ℂ⁡[XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]→≅ℂ​[RSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]SL2⁡(ℂ).\tau^{*}:\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathbb{C}[R_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]^{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}.

The term character variety does not require this affine algebraic set to be irreducible.

Lemma 3.9 (Sikora [35, Proposition 2]).

Suppose K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} is a knot. Then we have

ℂ⁡[XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]≅ℂ​[RSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]SL2⁡(ℂ)=TSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]\cong\mathbb{C}[R_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]^{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}=T_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)

where TSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)T_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) is the trace algebra as in Definition 3.7.

Remark 3.10.

A main ingredient of the proof of Proposition 4.8 below is the work by Ohtsuki [30]. Ohtsuki’s work then depends on a source paper by Culler–Shalen [17]. In [17], the character variety XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) is defined essentially as above, but with the trace algebra TSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)T_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K), rather than the SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})-invariant regular functions. We remark that Culler–Shalen’s original construct coincides with what we defined in Definition 3.8, as a corollary to Lemma 3.9.

Lemma 3.11.

Suppose K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} is a knot. Then there is a canonical bijection between the set XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) and the set of all characters {χρ}ρ∈RSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)\{\chi_{\rho}\}_{\rho\in R_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)}.

Proof.

Since τ\tau is surjective, every point is τ⁡(ρ)\tau(\rho) for some representation ρ\rho. Two representations have the same image under τ\tau precisely when all invariant regular functions agree on them. By Lemma 3.9, this is equivalent to the equality of all their traces, that is, to equality of their characters. ∎

With the above lemma at hand, we may write an element of the character variety XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) as χρ\chi_{\rho}. In particular, we have the following definition.

Definition 3.12.

Suppose K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} is a knot. Use the fixed peripheral system (mK,ℓK)(m_{K},\ell_{K}) with the preferred zero-linking longitude. We regard mKm_{K} and ℓK\ell_{K} as commuting elements in the knot group πK\pi_{K}. For (p,q)∈ℤ2(p,q)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}, we define

Ip,q=(tmKp​ℓKq)2−4.I_{p,q}=\left(t_{m_{K}^{p}\ell_{K}^{q}}\right)^{2}-4.

Note the trace functions are regular functions on XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) and so is Ip,qI_{p,q}.

3.2.1. PSL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) character variety

By definition PSL2⁡(ℂ)=SL2⁡(ℂ)/{±1}\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})=\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})/\{\pm 1\}, and there is an algebraic group isomorphism PSL2⁡(ℂ)≅SO3⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})\cong\operatorname{SO}_{3}(\mathbb{C}). This isomorphism provides us with the facts we will need to construct the character variety: PSL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) is reductive and RPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)R_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) is indeed an affine algebraic set (cf. [25, Section 2]).

Definition 3.13.

Suppose K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} is a knot. Define

RPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)=Hom⁡(πK,PSL2⁡(ℂ)).R_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)=\operatorname{Hom}(\pi_{K},\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})).

Define its PSL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) character variety XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) to be the affine algebraic set arising from a construction similar to that in Section 3.2, which has coordinate ring

ℂ⁡[XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]≅ℂ​[RPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]PSL2⁡(ℂ),\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]\cong\mathbb{C}[R_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]^{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})},

and admits a surjective regular map τ^:RPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)→XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)\hat{\tau}:R_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)\to X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K).

Definition 3.14.

Suppose K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} is a knot. For ρ∈RPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)\rho\in R_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) define the character associated to it as

χρ:πK→ℂ\chi_{\rho}:\pi_{K}\to\mathbb{C}

where χρ​(g)=tr⁡(ρ⁡(g))2\chi_{\rho}(g)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(g))^{2}. Note tr⁡(ρ⁡(g))\operatorname{tr}(\rho(g)) itself is not defined. More precisely, we write tr⁡(ρ⁡(g))2=tr⁡(A)2\operatorname{tr}(\rho(g))^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(A)^{2} where AA is a lift of ρ⁡(g)\rho(g) in SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}). This lift is determined up to a sign but taking the square resolves the ambiguity. Similarly, for an element g∈πKg\in\pi_{K} we define the square trace function associated to gg as t^g​(ρ)=tr⁡(ρ⁡(g))2\hat{t}_{g}(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(g))^{2}. Clearly, t^g\hat{t}_{g} are PSL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) invariant and hence become regular functions on XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K).

Lemma 3.15 (Heusener–Porti [25, Theorem 1.3 and Proposition 2.2]).

The square trace functions t^g\hat{t}_{g} for all g∈πKg\in\pi_{K} generate ℂ​[RPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]PSL2⁡(ℂ)\mathbb{C}[R_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]^{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}. Consequently, there is a (canonical) bijection between the set of all characters and the set XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K), which identifies χρ\chi_{\rho} with τ^​(ρ)\hat{\tau}(\rho) for any ρ∈RPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)\rho\in R_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K).

For the comparison below, we use finite morphisms between affine algebraic sets, without requiring these sets to be irreducible. We need to align the terminology in this paper with that in [19]: (1) Affine algebraic sets as defined in Section 2.4 are algebraic varieties in [19, Chapter 1, Observations 4.19 and 4.39]. (2) A regular map between two affine algebraic sets as in Section 2.4 is a morphism between algebraic varieties as in [19, Chapter 1, Definitions 3.28 and 4.37, Observation 3.29, and Corollary 3.38]. (3) Such a map is finite in the sense of [19, Definition 4.74] if the coordinate ring of its source is finitely generated as a module over the coordinate ring of its target via pullback; the global coordinate rings then provide the required trivial affine cover.

Lemma 3.16.

Suppose K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} is a knot. Then there is a surjective regular map (cf. Section 2.4) ψ:XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)→XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)\psi:X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)\to X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) such that the coordinate ring ℂ​[XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)] is a finitely generated ℂ​[XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]-module via the pullback

ψ∗:ℂ⁡[XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]→ℂ⁡[XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)].\psi^{*}:\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]\to\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)].
Proof.

First note that for the knot group πK\pi_{K}, we have H2​(πK,ℤ/2​ℤ)=0H^{2}(\pi_{K};\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})=0 (cf. the discussion before [12, Lemma 3.3]), and hence any PSL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) representation lifts to an SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) representation (cf. [25, Section 4]). Then Heusener–Porti [25, Proposition 4.2] supply the identification of XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) with the GIT quotient

XPSL2⁡(ℂ)(K)≅XSL2⁡(ℂ)(K)//H1(πK;ℤ/2ℤ).X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)\cong X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)//H^{1}(\pi_{K};\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}).

Note that H1​(πK,ℤ/2​ℤ)=Hom⁡(πK,ℤ/2​ℤ)=ℤ/2​ℤ={±1}H^{1}(\pi_{K};\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})=\operatorname{Hom}(\pi_{K},\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}=\{\pm 1\}. So we obtain a regular map

ψ:XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)→XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)\psi:X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)\to X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)

whose pullback provides an identification

ψ∗:ℂ⁡[XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]≅ℂ​[XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]{±1}\psi^{*}:\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]\cong\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]^{\{\pm 1\}}

Then ℂ​[XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)] is indeed a finitely generated module over ℂ​[XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]{±1}\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]^{\{\pm 1\}}: let tg1,⋯,tgnt_{g_{1}},\cdots,t_{g_{n}} be a set of (SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})) trace functions that generate ℂ​[XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)] as a ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra. Then we know tgi2∈ℂ​[XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]{±1}t_{g_{i}}^{2}\in\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]^{\{\pm 1\}}, and hence tg1ε1⋯tgnεnt_{g_{1}}^{\varepsilon_{1}}\cdots t_{g_{n}}^{\varepsilon_{n}} for all εi∈{0,1}\varepsilon_{i}\in\{0,1\} generate ℂ​[XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)] as a ℂ​[XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]{±1}\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]^{\{\pm 1\}}-module. ∎

Remark 3.17.

We now provide a concrete description of the map ψ\psi constructed above. From Lemma 3.11 and Lemma 3.15, we can identify points in the character variety with characters. If ρ∈RSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)\rho\in R_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) is an SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) representation, it naturally induces a PSL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) representation ρ^\hat{\rho} by composing with the natural quotient map SL2⁡(ℂ)→PSL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})\to\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}). Then in terms of characters, ψ⁡(χρ)=χρ^\psi(\chi_{\rho})=\chi_{\hat{\rho}}.

Corollary 3.18.

Suppose D⊂XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)D\subset X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) is a one-dimensional irreducible Zariski-closed subset. Then there exists a one-dimensional irreducible Zariski-closed subset C⊂XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)C\subset X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) such that

ψ|C:C→D\psi|_{C}:C\to D

is a surjective morphism.

Proof.

Let C1,⋯,CnC_{1},\cdots,C_{n} be the irreducible components of ψ−1​(D)\psi^{-1}(D) (by [23, Chapter I, Corollary 1.6] there are finitely many). By Lemma 3.16 and the convention above, ψ\psi is finite.

Thus, we apply [19, Chapter 1, Theorem 4.93] and conclude that ψ\psi is a closed map, so each ψ⁡(Ci)\psi(C_{i}) is a closed subset of DD. By the definition of irreducibility in Section 2.4, there exists an index ii such that ψ⁡(Ci)=D\psi(C_{i})=D. Hence take C=CiC=C_{i}. It remains to show that CC is indeed a curve. By [19, Chapter 1, Theorem 4.93], ψ|C\psi|_{C} is a finite map. Then [19, Chapter 1, Lemma 4.95] implies that CC must be a curve. ∎

Remark 3.19.

Ip,qI_{p,q} was originally defined on XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) as an element in the coordinate ring. However, Lemma 3.16 canonically identifies ℂ​[XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)] as the invariant subring ℂ​[XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)]{±1}\mathbb{C}[X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)]^{\{\pm 1\}}, and Ip,qI_{p,q} lies inside that subring. So, abusing notation, we write Ip,qI_{p,q} as a polynomial function on XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) as well, and we have ψ∗​Ip,q=Ip,q\psi^{*}I_{p,q}=I_{p,q} where the function Ip,qI_{p,q} on the left-hand side is a polynomial function on XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) while the one on the right-hand side is on XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K).

3.3. Ohtsuki’s result

In this section, we summarize key ingredients from Ohtsuki [30]. Let KK be a 22-bridge knot, then its fundamental group has a presentation of the form

πK=⟨u,v|wu=vw⟩\pi_{K}=\langle u,v~|~wu=vw\rangle

for a suitable word ww in uu and vv. Ohtsuki defines RR to be the dimension ≥4\geq 4 components of the variety of all PSL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) representations, and XX to be the set of all conjugacy classes of elements in RR. For a generic element [ρ]∈X[\rho]\in X, he defined

τ=2​tr⁡(U~​V~)−(tr⁡U~)2(tr⁡U~)2−4​ and ​ξ=−2(tr⁡(U~))2−4.\tau=\frac{2\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde{U}\widetilde{V})-(\operatorname{tr}\widetilde{U})^{2}}{(\operatorname{tr}\widetilde{U})^{2}-4}\text{ and }\xi=\frac{-2}{({\rm tr}(\widetilde{U}))^{2}-4}.

Here we take U=ρ⁡(u)U=\rho(u), V=ρ⁡(v)V=\rho(v) and SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})-lifts U~\widetilde{U} and V~\widetilde{V} which are conjugate to each other. Ohtsuki showed that these coordinates identify the set of generic irreducible points (i.e., conjugacy classes) of XX with a Zariski-open subset 𝒞⁡(K)\mathcal{C}(K) of the one-dimensional algebraic set in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} cut out by z⁡(τ,ξ)=0z(\tau,\xi)=0. The following lemma is implicit in his paper.

Lemma 3.20.

For any element g∈πKg\in\pi_{K}, the map t^g:𝒞⁡(K)→ℂ\hat{t}_{g}:\mathcal{C}(K)\to\mathbb{C} defined by

t^g​([ρ])=(tr⁡(ρ⁡(g)))2\hat{t}_{g}([\rho])=({\rm tr}(\rho(g)))^{2}

is regular on 𝒞⁡(K)\mathcal{C}(K).

The above lemma is not explicitly proved, but is essentially a corollary to [30, Lemma 1.2] with proof similar to that of [30, Lemma 4.9]. As a corollary, Ohtsuki stated that functions

Ip,qO​h​([ρ])=(tr⁡(ρ⁡(mKp​ℓKq)))2−4.I^{Oh}_{p,q}([\rho])=\bigg({\rm tr}(\rho(m_{K}^{p}\ell_{K}^{q}))\bigg)^{2}-4.

for all (p,q)∈ℤ2(p,q)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2} are all regular on 𝒞⁡(K)\mathcal{C}(K). The key ingredient is the following.

Lemma 3.21.

Suppose K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} is a 22-bridge knot and r≠0r\neq 0 is the boundary slope of a non-closed oriented essential (i.e., incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and non-boundary-parallel) properly embedded orientable surface in the knot complement, then there exists an irreducible component X0{X}_{0} of 𝒞⁡(K)\mathcal{C}(K), a smooth projective model X~0\widetilde{X}_{0} with a point Q∈X~0Q\in\widetilde{X}_{0}, and ε0∈{1,2}\varepsilon_{0}\in\{1,2\} such that for any (p,q)∈ℤ2(p,q)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}, we have

poleQ​(Ip,qO​h|X0)=ε0⋅|p−r​q|.{\rm pole}_{Q}(I^{Oh}_{p,q}|_{{X}_{0}})=\varepsilon_{0}\cdot|p-rq|.
Proof.

By Hatcher–Thurston’s classification (cf. [24, Theorem 1]), as recalled in [30, Section 2], there is a continued fraction [nj][n_{j}], with |nj|≥2|n_{j}|\geq 2 for every jj, such that r=N[nj]r=N_{[n_{j}]} (cf. [30, Section 2] for definition). The unique continued fraction expansion [nj][n_{j}] whose coefficients are all even has corresponding N[nj]=0N_{[n_{j}]}=0. Since r≠0r\neq 0, in an expansion [nj][n_{j}] such that r=N[nj]r=N_{[n_{j}]}, some njn_{j} is odd. Consequently, choosing each residue kj∈ℤ/(nj)k_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}/(n_{j}) to be the class of 11 gives a tuple allowed by Ohtsuki’s Theorem 5.1. Thus we can apply that theorem and the pole-order formula immediately preceding Proposition 5.2 and take X0X_{0}, QQ and ε0∈{1,2}\varepsilon_{0}\in\{1,2\} as desired. ∎

4. Two-bridge knots and their Whitehead doubles

4.1. Whitehead-iterable branches

For every finite NN, the set 𝒮N\mathcal{S}_{N} of Section 2.4 contains a dense open subset of the peripheral torus. We now give a condition ensuring that a curve of actual augmentation points meets these sets. The condition is expressed in terms of valuations on a smooth projective model, using the terminology of the preceding section.

We work over ℂ\mathbb{C} and write

T=(ℂ∗)(μ,η)2,η=λ2.T=(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{2}_{(\mu,\eta)},\qquad\eta=\lambda^{2}.

We use 𝒮N\mathcal{S}_{N} and 𝒢N\mathcal{G}_{N} for the sets already defined in Section 2.4; in particular, 𝒢N⊆𝒮N\mathcal{G}_{N}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{N}.

Definition 4.1.

Let C⊂TC\subset T be an irreducible algebraic curve. We say that CC has a Whitehead-iterable branch (and iterable branch for short), if CC admits an ideal point PP with νP​(μ)=−p\nu_{P}(\mu)=-p and νP​(η)=q\nu_{P}(\eta)=q for (p,q)∈ℤ2(p,q)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2} such that

(4.1) OPENp>0​ and (either ​q>p​or​q<0).p>0\text{ and (either }q>p~{\rm or}~q<0).

Now for each point (μ,η)(\mu,\eta), we have one-step correspondence (μ~,λ~)(\widetilde{\mu},\widetilde{\lambda}) as in (2.16). Since μ~\widetilde{\mu} is defined via a quadratic equation, in general it is not a rational function on the original CC, so the valuation ν\nu is not directly applicable for μ~\widetilde{\mu}. There are two routes to settle this issue: (1) Take a suitable (branched) double cover of CC so that (μ~,λ~)(\widetilde{\mu},\widetilde{\lambda}) are well defined rational functions, and work with valuations of them, and (2) switch to use complex analytical topology. The two routes will lead to equivalent arguments, and we adopt (2).

As in Definition 3.6, in a small enough complex-analytical neighborhood of the ideal point PP of CC, we have a local Puiseux parameter ss. Thus we introduce the following notation for a local (near PP) meromorphic function ff with at most a pole at s=0s=0: one can express such an ff that is not identically zero as

f=sr⋅h⁡(s)f=s^{r}\cdot h(s)

where r∈ℤr\in\mathbb{Z} and hh is holomorphic with h⁡(0)≠0h(0)\neq 0. Then we write 𝔬⁡(f)=r\mathfrak{o}(f)=r. Also define 𝔬⁡(0)=+∞\mathfrak{o}(0)=+\infty. Note μ\mu and η\eta restrict to meromorphic functions near s=0s=0, and the above valuation, via Lemma 3.5, can be restated as

𝔬⁡(μ)=−p​and​𝔬​(η)=q.\mathfrak{o}(\mu)=-p\ \text{and}\ \mathfrak{o}(\eta)=q.

Furthermore, we have the following properties for 𝔬\mathfrak{o}:

  • •

    𝔬⁡(c)=0\mathfrak{o}(c)=0 for c∈ℂ∗c\in\mathbb{C}^{*}.

  • •

    𝔬⁡(f⋅g)=𝔬⁡(f)+𝔬⁡(g)\mathfrak{o}(f\cdot g)=\mathfrak{o}(f)+\mathfrak{o}(g).

  • •

    𝔬⁡(f+g)≥min⁡{𝔬⁡(f),𝔬⁡(g)}\mathfrak{o}(f+g)\geq\min\{\mathfrak{o}(f),\mathfrak{o}(g)\}, with equality whenever 𝔬⁡(f)≠𝔬⁡(g)\mathfrak{o}(f)\neq\mathfrak{o}(g).

Theorem 4.2.

Let C⊂TC\subset T be an irreducible algebraic curve with an iterable branch. For every integer N≥0N\geq 0, the intersection C∩𝒮NC\cap\mathcal{S}_{N} (cf. Section 2.4) contains a nonempty Zariski-open subset of CC.

Proof.

Let P∈C~P\in\widetilde{C} be the ideal point specified by the iterable branch, and let uu be a local parameter at PP. On a sufficiently small parameter, write η⁡(u)=uq​h​(u)2\eta(u)=u^{q}h(u)^{2}, where hh is holomorphic near 00 and h⁡(0)≠0h(0)\neq 0. On the covering disk given by u=s2u=s^{2}, define

μ0​(s):=μ⁡(s2),λ0​(s):=sq​h​(s2),η0​(s):=λ0​(s)2=η⁡(s2).\mu_{0}(s):=\mu(s^{2}),\qquad\lambda_{0}(s):=s^{q}h(s^{2}),\qquad\eta_{0}(s):=\lambda_{0}(s)^{2}=\eta(s^{2}).

Throughout this proof, 𝔬\mathfrak{o} denotes the order at s=0s=0 on this covering disk. Thus

−𝔬⁡(μ0)=2​p,𝔬⁡(η0)=2​q.-\mathfrak{o}(\mu_{0})=2p,\qquad\mathfrak{o}(\eta_{0})=2q.

We will establish the following claim by induction via the correspondence 𝒲\mathcal{W} introduced in Section 2.4.

Claim. For any N∈ℤ≥0N\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, there exists εN>0\varepsilon_{N}>0 such that on DεN={z∈ℂ||z|<εN}D_{\varepsilon_{N}}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}~|~|z|<\varepsilon_{N}\}, there exist meromorphic functions μN​(s)\mu_{N}(s), λN​(s)\lambda_{N}(s) with only possible pole at s=0s=0,

ηN:=λN2,pN:=−𝔬⁡(μN),and​qN:=𝔬⁡(ηN)\eta_{N}:=\lambda_{N}^{2},~p_{N}:=-\mathfrak{o}(\mu_{N}),\ \text{and}\ q_{N}:=\mathfrak{o}(\eta_{N})
