Remark 4.3.

The passage to the covering disk u=s2u=s^{2} ensures the existence of the initial meromorphic λ0\lambda_{0}. Although η\eta is meromorphic in the original parameter uu, its order qq may be odd, whereas the square of a meromorphic function has even order. After the substitution u=s2u=s^{2}, the function η0​(s)=η⁡(s2)\eta_{0}(s)=\eta(s^{2}) has order 2​q2q and hence admits a meromorphic square root on a sufficiently small disk. If qq is even, this covering substitution can be omitted. This applies, for example, to the branch constructed for a 22-bridge knot in Theorem 4.6, since q=r​pq=rp, where rr is an even integer.

Definition 4.4.

Let KK be a knot. An irreducible curve C⊂TC\subset T is an actual rank-dd augmentation peripheral curve for KK if it contains a Zariski-dense subset CactC^{\mathrm{act}} such that every point of CactC^{\mathrm{act}} is of the form

(μ,η)=(ϵ⁡(μ),ϵ​(λ)2)(\mu,\eta)=\bigl(\epsilon(\mu),\epsilon(\lambda)^{2}\bigr)

for a rank-dd augmentation ϵ\epsilon of KK with ϵ⁡(μ)≠1\epsilon(\mu)\neq 1.

Under the augmentation–sheaf correspondence, these points are (μ,λ2)(\mu,\lambda^{2}), where (μ,λ)(\mu,\lambda) are the peripheral data of irreducible dd-dimensional diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representations. The word “actual” distinguishes these points from points introduced only by taking a Zariski closure.

Corollary 4.5.

Suppose that KK has an actual rank-dd augmentation peripheral curve with an iterable branch. Then, for every N≥0N\geq 0,

ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))≥2N​d.\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\geq 2^{N}d.

If d=b⁡(K)d=b(K), then

ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))=mr⁡(WhN⁡(K))=b⁡(WhN⁡(K))=2N​b​(K).\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=\operatorname{mr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=b(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=2^{N}b(K).
Proof.

By Theorem 4.2, C∩𝒮NC\cap\mathcal{S}_{N} contains a nonempty open subset of CC. This subset meets CactC^{\mathrm{act}}. Choose a rank-dd augmentation giving such a point and apply Proposition 2.16. This proves the lower bound. When d=b⁡(K)d=b(K), Corollary 2.17 gives all three equalities. ∎

The actual augmentation point chosen in this proof may depend on NN. The result does not require a single point to realize all the iterations.

4.2. Two-bridge knots admit iterable branches

Throughout this section, we take KK to be a 22-bridge knot. The goal of this section is to establish the following theorem

Theorem 4.6.

Any 22-bridge knot admits an actual rank-22 augmentation peripheral curve as in Definition 4.4 with an iterable branch as in Definition 4.1.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

The combination of Theorem 4.6 and Corollary 4.5 directly implies

ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))=mr⁡(WhN⁡(K))=b⁡(WhN⁡(K))=2N+1\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=\operatorname{mr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=b(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=2^{N+1}

for every N≥0N\geq 0. ∎

The rest of the section is dedicated to the proof of Theorem 4.6. We need several preparations. First, a properly embedded surface S⊂E⁡(K)=S3−int⁡(N⁡(K))S\subset E(K)=S^{3}-{\rm int}(N(K)) is said to be essential if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and non-boundary-parallel. We have the following existence result.

Lemma 4.7.

Suppose K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} is a 22-bridge knot. Then there exists an oriented essential non-closed properly embedded surface SS in its knot complement and ∂S\partial S has slope rr which is an even non-zero integer.

Proof.

First, [28, Theorem 1] shows that the diameter of the set of boundary slopes is positive for a 22-bridge knot KK. Since a minimal genus Seifert surface has boundary slope 00, there must exist a non-zero boundary slope rr. Furthermore, [28, Section 1] indicates that such an rr can be picked to be an even integer. ∎

Proposition 4.8.

Suppose K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} is a nontrivial 22-bridge knot. Then there exist a nonzero even boundary slope rr, a one-dimensional irreducible Zariski-closed subset C′⊂XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)C^{\prime}\subset X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K), an ideal point QQ of the smooth projective model C~′\widetilde{C}^{\prime} of C′C^{\prime}, and a positive rational number ε\varepsilon, such that for any (p,q)∈ℤ2(p,q)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2} we have

poleQ⁡(Ip,q|C′)=ε⋅|p−r​q|.\operatorname{pole}_{Q}(I_{p,q}|_{C^{\prime}})=\varepsilon\cdot|p-rq|.

Here, Ip,qI_{p,q} is a regular function on XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) introduced in Definition 3.12, and we view Ip,q|C′I_{p,q}|_{C^{\prime}} as a rational function on C~′\widetilde{C}^{\prime}.

We first show that there exists a 1-dimensional irreducible Zariski-closed subset D⊂XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)D\subset X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K), and an ideal point QQ of its smooth projective model D~\widetilde{D}, such that there exists a positive integer ε′\varepsilon^{\prime} and for any (p,q)∈ℤ2(p,q)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}, we have

poleQ​(Ip,q|D)=ε′⋅|p−r​q|.{\rm pole}_{Q}(I_{p,q}|_{D})=\varepsilon^{\prime}\cdot|p-rq|.

We proceed with the non-zero even boundary slope rr obtained from Lemma 4.7. Lemma 3.21 then applies and produces a quasi-affine curve X0X_{0} with a point QQ in its smooth projective model X~0\widetilde{X}_{0} and the pole order formula

(4.4) poleQ​(Ip,qO​h|X0)=ε0⋅|p−r​q|.{\rm pole}_{Q}(I^{Oh}_{p,q}|_{X_{0}})=\varepsilon_{0}\cdot|p-rq|.

However, we still need a transition from Ohtsuki’s space XX to our PSL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) character variety. Ohtsuki defined elements in XX as conjugation classes of representations ρ∈RPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)\rho\in R_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K), and our map τ^:RPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)→XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)\hat{\tau}:R_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)\to X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) defined as in Definition 3.13 with a chosen set of square trace functions generating the coordinate ring naturally induces a map, which, by abusing notation, we still denote by τ^:X0→XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)\hat{\tau}:X_{0}\to X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K). One core identity that is straightforward from the construction is that

Ip,qO​h=Ip,q∘τ^I_{p,q}^{Oh}=I_{p,q}\circ\widehat{\tau}

Next, take D=τ^​(X0)¯D=\overline{\hat{\tau}(X_{0})} to be the Zariski-closure of the image inside XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K). It is irreducible since X0X_{0} is. [25, Corollary 3.6] states that the irreducible locus XPSL2⁡(ℂ)i​r​r​(K)⊂XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X^{irr}_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K)\subset X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) is Zariski open. Thus, τ^−1​(Di​r​r)\hat{\tau}^{-1}(D^{irr}) is open, and we show that it is not empty in X0X_{0}. Suppose, on the contrary, that every element [ρ]∈X0[\rho]\in X_{0} is reducible. Then for any [ρ]∈X0[\rho]\in X_{0}, τ^​([ρ])=χρ\hat{\tau}([\rho])=\chi_{\rho} is a reducible character. [25, Remark 3.7] implies that the same χρ\chi_{\rho} can also be represented by an abelian representation ρ′\rho^{\prime}: χρ=χρ′\chi_{\rho}=\chi_{\rho^{\prime}}. Thus, the curve DD and its ideal point QQ are the desired data on XPSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K), i.e., for any (p,q)∈ℤ2(p,q)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}, we have

poleQ​(Ip,q|D)=ε′⋅|p−r​q|.{\rm pole}_{Q}(I_{p,q}|_{D})=\varepsilon^{\prime}\cdot|p-rq|.

We can then lift DD to the desired curve C′C^{\prime} in XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) via Corollary 3.18. The ideal point and associated valuation are liftable as well by Lemma 3.2 and Lemma 3.4. This completes the proof. ∎

For a 2-bridge knot KK, let C′⊂XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)C^{\prime}\subset X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) be the curve supplied by Proposition 4.8, and use the fixed peripheral system (mK,ℓK)(m_{K},\ell_{K}) . We now proceed to construct the desired curve C⊂TC\subset T (with iterable branch) to establish Theorem 4.6. The basic idea is to twist an SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) representation to obtain a μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation, though a detailed construction shall pass to what we call the eigenvalue cover EE of C′C^{\prime}. A conceptual diagram is the following.

C′←𝜋E→𝜁C⊂T.C^{\prime}\xlongleftarrow{\pi}E\xlongrightarrow{\zeta}C\subset T.

Next, we construct EE. First, Culler–Shalen [17, Proof of Corollary 1.4.5] show that characters from irreducible representations form a Zariski-open subset of XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K). Hence on C′C^{\prime} they form a possibly empty open subset UU. We argue that this is nonempty. Otherwise all characters come from reducible SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) representations. Such a representation can be written in upper-triangular form, and its diagonal part is an abelian representation with the same character. Yet for an abelian representation ℓK\ell_{K} is sent to I2I_{2}, so Ir,1=Ir,0I_{r,1}=I_{r,0}, violating the pole order formula in Proposition 4.8. Thus U⊂C′U\subset C^{\prime} is a non-empty and hence dense open subset of C′C^{\prime}.

Define X⊂C′×(ℂ∗)2X\subset C^{\prime}\times(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{2} by the equations

(4.5) M2−tmK​M+1\displaystyle M^{2}-t_{m_{K}}M+1 =0\displaystyle=0
L2−tℓK​L+1\displaystyle L^{2}-t_{\ell_{K}}L+1 =0\displaystyle=0
(M​L)2−tmK​ℓK​(M​L)+1\displaystyle(ML)^{2}-t_{m_{K}\ell_{K}}(ML)+1 =0\displaystyle=0

XX is an affine algebraic set, since the trace functions are polynomial functions on XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) and hence on C′C^{\prime}. The projection π:X→C′\pi:X\to C^{\prime} is surjective: mKm_{K} and ℓK\ell_{K} commute in πK\pi_{K} by assumption, so for a representation ρ\rho we can always take the eigenvalues of ρ⁡(mK)\rho(m_{K}) and ρ⁡(ℓK)\rho({\ell_{K}}) on a common eigenline to satisfy Equation (4.5). Note the third equation requires the compatibility between MM and LL. The defining equations also imply that ℂ⁡[X]\mathbb{C}[X] is a finitely generated module over ℂ⁡[C′]\mathbb{C}[C^{\prime}] via the pullback π∗\pi^{*}: four generators are enough: 1,M,L,M​L1,M,L,ML. As a result, the proof of Corollary 3.18 applies again: there exists an irreducible Zariski-closed subset E⊂XE\subset X such that π⁡(E)=C′\pi(E)=C^{\prime}. ℂ⁡[E]\mathbb{C}[E] is a quotient of ℂ⁡[X]\mathbb{C}[X], so it is also a finitely generated module over ℂ⁡[C′]\mathbb{C}[C^{\prime}] via pullback. Then EE is itself an algebraic curve. We have the following property of EE.

Lemma 4.9.

Let K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} be a 22-bridge knot. Let rr be a non-zero even boundary slope arising from Lemma 4.7, C′⊂XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)C^{\prime}\subset X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) be the algebraic curve arising from Proposition 4.8 and π:E→C′\pi:E\to C^{\prime} be the eigenvalue cover of C′C^{\prime} together with regular functions MM and LL as above. Then EE admits an ideal point Q′Q^{\prime} such that

(4.6) νQ′​(M)≠0,r​νQ′​(M)+νQ′​(L)=0.\nu_{Q^{\prime}}(M)\neq 0,~r\nu_{Q^{\prime}}(M)+\nu_{Q^{\prime}}(L)=0.
Proof.

Further pulling it back, ϕ~E∗​π∗​I1,0\tilde{\phi}_{E}^{*}\pi^{*}I_{1,0} is a regular function on a Zariski-open neighborhood of Q′Q^{\prime} so it has pole order 00. On the other hand, Lemma 3.4 implies that

E0={e∈E:M​(e)2≠1}E_{0}=\{e\in E:M(e)^{2}\neq 1\}

is a nonempty open subset of EE.

The third equation in (4.5) ensures that MM and LL belong to the same peripheral eigenline on E0E_{0}. To see this, fix e∈E0e\in E_{0} and a representation of the character π⁡(e)\pi(e). Write α=M⁡(e)\alpha=M(e). In a basis of meridian eigenvectors, the meridian and longitude matrices are diag⁡(α,α−1)\operatorname{diag}(\alpha,\alpha^{-1}) and diag⁡(β,β−1)\operatorname{diag}(\beta,\beta^{-1}), respectively. π∗​Ip,q=(Mp​Lq−M−p​L−q)2((p,q)∈ℤ2).\pi^{*}I_{p,q}=(M^{p}L^{q}-M^{-p}L^{-q})^{2}\qquad((p,q)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}).

∎

Proof of Theorem 4.6.

Let KK be a 2-bridge knot, rr be a non-zero even integral boundary slope as in Lemma 4.7, (mK,ℓK)(m_{K},\ell_{K}) be chosen peripheral data, and C′⊂XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)C^{\prime}\subset X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) be an irreducible algebraic curve with ideal point QQ with special pole order formula supplied by Proposition 4.8. Let π:E→C′\pi:E\to C^{\prime} be the eigenvalue cover constructed as above, together with regular functions MM and LL, and EE’s smooth projective model (E~,ϕ~E)(\widetilde{E},\tilde{\phi}_{E}) with ideal point Q′∈E~Q^{\prime}\in\widetilde{E} and valuation data as in Lemma 4.9.

We now construct the actual rank-22 augmentation peripheral curve C⊂TC\subset T as follows. Take σ=1\sigma=1 if νQ′​(M)<0\nu_{Q^{\prime}}(M)<0 and σ=−1\sigma=-1 otherwise. We define a map ζ:E→T=(ℂ∗)(μ,η)2\zeta:E\to T=(\mathbb{C}^{*})_{(\mu,\eta)}^{2} by μ=M2​σ\mu=M^{2\sigma} and η=L2​σ\eta=L^{2\sigma}. Let C⊂TC\subset T be the Zariski closure of im⁡ζ\operatorname{im}\zeta. Since EE is irreducible, so is CC. The dimension theorem of Ferrer Santos–Rittatore [19, Chapter 1, Theorem 4.84] then implies that CC has dimension at most 11. Dimension 00 implies that CC must be a single point (see Section 2.4). If CC were a point, then the map ζ\zeta would be constant. Yet (viewing μ\mu as a regular function on EE) νQ′​(μ)=2​σ⋅νQ′​(M)<0\nu_{Q^{\prime}}(\mu)=2\sigma\cdot\nu_{Q^{\prime}}(M)<0 so ζ\zeta is not constant. Consequently, CC is an affine algebraic curve. Take its smooth projective model (C~,ϕ~C)(\widetilde{C},\tilde{\phi}_{C}). Lemma 3.2 produces a compatible surjective morphism E~→C~\widetilde{E}\to\widetilde{C}. Taking PP to be the image of Q′Q^{\prime} under this morphism, Lemma 3.4 now implies that there exists a positive ε\varepsilon such that

−p=νP​(μ)=ε⋅2​σ⋅νQ′​(M)<0.-p=\nu_{P}(\mu)=\varepsilon\cdot 2\sigma\cdot\nu_{Q^{\prime}}(M)<0.

The same lemma gives

q=νP​(η)=ε⋅2​σ⋅νQ′​(L),qp=r.q=\nu_{P}(\eta)=\varepsilon\cdot 2\sigma\cdot\nu_{Q^{\prime}}(L),\qquad\frac{q}{p}=r.

The pole of the regular function μ\mu at PP shows that PP is an ideal point of CC. Since p>0p>0 and r∉[0,1]r\notin[0,1], either q>pq>p or q<0q<0.

As a consequence, with Lemma 3.5, we conclude that CC has an iterable branch as defined in Definition 4.1. It remains to show that CC provides an actual rank-two augmentation peripheral curve, as in Definition 4.4.

First, note there is a dense open subset U⊂C′⊂XSL2⁡(ℂ)​(K)U\subset C^{\prime}\subset X_{\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}(K) consisting of characters of irreducible representations. Pulling it back via the surjective π\pi, we obtain an open dense subset V′=π−1​(U)⊂EV^{\prime}=\pi^{-1}(U)\subset E. We restrict V′V^{\prime} to the nonempty open subset where M,LM,L belong to a common peripheral eigenline, and further exclude the closed subsets M=±1M=\pm 1. Call the resulting subset VV. It is still open, and note that EE is not fully contained in M=±1M=\pm 1 since νQ′​(M)≠0\nu_{Q^{\prime}}(M)\neq 0 by Lemma 4.9. Hence we conclude that V⊂EV\subset E is an open and dense subset.

For e∈Ve\in V, choose an irreducible representation ρe\rho_{e} with character π⁡(e)\pi(e), and write α=M⁡(e)\alpha=M(e) and β=L⁡(e)\beta=L(e). Let ab:πK→ℤ\operatorname{ab}:\pi_{K}\to\mathbb{Z} be the abelianization with ab⁡(mK)=1\operatorname{ab}(m_{K})=1. Define the scalar twist ρeσ:πK→GL⁡(ℂ2)\rho_{e}^{\sigma}\colon\pi_{K}\to\operatorname{GL}(\mathbb{C}^{2}) by

ρeσ​(g)=ασ​ab⁡(g)​ρe​(g).\rho_{e}^{\sigma}(g)=\alpha^{\sigma\operatorname{ab}(g)}\rho_{e}(g).

After this scalar twist, the two eigenvalues of the meridian are 11 and α2​σ\alpha^{2\sigma}, and hence an irreducible SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) representation yields an irreducible two-dimensional diagonalizable μ​rk\mu\operatorname{rk}-one representation. Since ab⁡(ℓK)=0\operatorname{ab}(\ell_{K})=0, the longitude eigenvalue on the distinguished meridian eigenline is βσ\beta^{\sigma}. The augmentation–representation correspondence therefore realizes

(μ⁡(e),η⁡(e))=(α2​σ,β2​σ)(\mu(e),\eta(e))=(\alpha^{2\sigma},\beta^{2\sigma})

as an actual rank-two augmentation peripheral point.

To conclude the proof, it remains to show that ζ⁡(V)\zeta(V) contains an open and dense subset of CC. Now the fact that VV is dense in EE implies that ζ⁡(V)\zeta(V) is dense in ζ⁡(E)\zeta(E), and hence dense in C=ζ⁡(E)¯C=\overline{\zeta(E)}. Thus the constructibility theorem of Ferrer Santos–Rittatore [19, Theorem 4.91] applies, and the proof is complete. ∎

Corollary 4.10.

Let KK be a nontrivial knot with mr⁡(K)=2\operatorname{mr}(K)=2. Then, for every N≥0N\geq 0,

ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))=mr⁡(WhN⁡(K))=b⁡(WhN⁡(K))=2N+1.\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=\operatorname{mr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=b(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=2^{N+1}.
Proof.

The two-meridian characterization of two-bridge knots [11, Corollary 3.3], with the orbifold theorem [9], implies that KK is two-bridge. Apply Theorem 1.1. ∎

5. Ordinary group rank

Having proved the two-bridge result, we compare it with ordinary group rank. Here generators are unrestricted: gr⁡(K)\operatorname{gr}(K) is the minimum cardinality of a generating set of πK\pi_{K}.

Proposition 5.1.

For every knot KK and every N≥0N\geq 0,

gr⁡(Wh⁡(K))≤gr⁡(K)+1,gr⁡(WhN⁡(K))≤gr⁡(K)+N.\operatorname{gr}(\operatorname{Wh}(K))\leq\operatorname{gr}(K)+1,\qquad\operatorname{gr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\leq\operatorname{gr}(K)+N.
Proof.

The relation ℓ𝒱​x2​ℓ𝒱−1=x1\ell_{\mathcal{V}}x_{2}\ell_{\mathcal{V}}^{-1}=x_{1} in (2.2) gives x2=ℓ𝒱−1​x1​ℓ𝒱x_{2}=\ell_{\mathcal{V}}^{-1}x_{1}\ell_{\mathcal{V}}. Thus x1x_{1} and ℓ𝒱\ell_{\mathcal{V}} generate the pattern group. In the satellite group, ℓ𝒱=ℓK\ell_{\mathcal{V}}=\ell_{K} belongs to the image of the companion group. It follows that πWh⁡(K)\pi_{\operatorname{Wh}(K)} is generated by this image and x1x_{1}. This proves the first inequality, and induction gives the second. ∎

For comparison, Gu–Wang–Zou [21, Proposition 1.3] prove that

gr⁡(WhN⁡(K))≥N+1\operatorname{gr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\geq N+1

for every nontrivial knot KK and N≥1N\geq 1. Each Whitehead layer contributes a hyperbolic piece to the JSJ decomposition, and their argument uses these pieces to bound the rank from below. Combining this with Proposition 5.1, we obtain

N+1≤gr⁡(WhN⁡(K))≤N+gr⁡(K),N≥1.N+1\leq\operatorname{gr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\leq N+\operatorname{gr}(K),\qquad N\geq 1.

In particular, for a fixed nontrivial KK,

limN→∞gr⁡(WhN⁡(K))N+1=1.\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{gr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))}{N+1}=1.

This asymptotic formula also appears in [21, Corollary 2.5], where the upper bound is expressed using tunnel number.

When KK is hyperbolic with tunnel number one, [21, Corollary 2.6] gives the exact value gr⁡(WhN⁡(K))=N+2\operatorname{gr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=N+2 for N≥1N\geq 1. In particular, for a hyperbolic two-bridge knot, Theorem 1.1 gives the comparison

gr⁡(WhN⁡(K))=N+2<2N+1=ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))=mr⁡(WhN⁡(K)),N≥1.\operatorname{gr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=N+2<2^{N+1}=\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))=\operatorname{mr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K)),\qquad N\geq 1.

The exact ordinary-rank formula here uses the hyperbolic hypothesis; we do not assert it for every two-bridge companion.

Corollary 5.2.

Suppose KK has a rank-dd augmentation ϵ\epsilon with ϵ⁡(μ)≠1\epsilon(\mu)\neq 1 and peripheral point in 𝒮N\mathcal{S}_{N}. If 2N​d≥gr⁡(K)+N2^{N}d\geq\operatorname{gr}(K)+N, then

gr⁡(WhN⁡(K))≤ar⁡(WhN⁡(K)).\operatorname{gr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\leq\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K)).
Proof.

Proposition 2.16 gives ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))≥2N​d\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\geq 2^{N}d, whereas Proposition 5.1 gives gr⁡(WhN⁡(K))≤gr⁡(K)+N\operatorname{gr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\leq\operatorname{gr}(K)+N. The numerical hypothesis compares these bounds. ∎

For a rank-two augmentation the numerical condition is gr⁡(K)≤2N+1−N\operatorname{gr}(K)\leq 2^{N+1}-N. In particular it is automatic when gr⁡(K)=2\operatorname{gr}(K)=2 and N≥1N\geq 1, provided the required peripheral point lies in 𝒮N\mathcal{S}_{N}. The existence of such a point, for each NN, is supplied by an actual rank-two augmentation peripheral curve with an iterable branch; see the proof of Corollary 4.5.

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

The unconditional upper bound is Proposition 5.1. Under the actual-curve hypothesis, Corollary 4.5 gives ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))≥2N​d\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\geq 2^{N}d for every N≥0N\geq 0. Consequently,

gr⁡(WhN⁡(K))≤gr⁡(K)+N≤2N​d≤ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))\operatorname{gr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\leq\operatorname{gr}(K)+N\leq 2^{N}d\leq\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))

whenever the middle inequality holds.

Finally, a nontrivial two-bridge knot has a two-generator nonabelian knot group, so gr⁡(K)=2\operatorname{gr}(K)=2. Theorem 1.1 and N+2≤2N+1N+2\leq 2^{N+1} yield the final assertion. ∎

Remark 5.3.

For a fixed knot with the actual-curve hypothesis and d>0d>0, the numerical condition in Theorem 1.2 holds for all sufficiently large NN. This conclusion depends on the curve hypothesis; the linear upper bound alone does not imply gr⁡(WhN⁡(K))≤ar⁡(WhN⁡(K))\operatorname{gr}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K))\leq\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}^{N}(K)).

6. The first Whitehead double of the square knot

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.3. Let

S:=T⁡(2,3)#T⁡(2,3)¯S:=T(2,3)\mathbin{\#}\overline{T(2,3)}

be the square knot. It has

ar⁡(S)=mr⁡(S)=b⁡(S)=3\operatorname{ar}(S)=\operatorname{mr}(S)=b(S)=3

where ar⁡(S)=2+2−1=3\operatorname{ar}(S)=2+2-1=3 is given by the formula in [16, Theorem 1.9], and b⁡(S)=2+2−1=3b(S)=2+2-1=3 is by [32].

For its untwisted Whitehead double Wh⁡(S)\operatorname{Wh}(S), Dutra’s bridge formula gives b⁡(Wh⁡(S))=2​b​(S)=6b(\operatorname{Wh}(S))=2b(S)=6 [18, Section 4]. In Section 6.1, we show that ar⁡(Wh⁡(S))≤5\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}(S))\leq 5, and in Section 6.2, we then use a finite quotient and group cohomology to show that its mr⁡(Wh⁡(S))=6\operatorname{mr}(\operatorname{Wh}(S))=6.

6.1. Augmentation rank of Wh⁡(S)\operatorname{Wh}(S)

The knot group of the square knot is

πS=⟨a,b,c∣aba=bab,aca=cac⟩,\pi_{S}=\langle a,b,c\mid aba=bab,\ aca=cac\rangle,

(6.1) πWh⁡(S)=⟨x1,x2,a,b,c,ℓ|a=x2​x1−1​x2−1​x1,ℓ​x2​ℓ−1=x1,[a,ℓ]=1,a​b​a=b​a​b,a​c​a=c​a​c,ℓ=(a​b)3(ac)−3⟩.\pi_{\operatorname{Wh}(S)}=\left\langle x_{1},x_{2},a,b,c,\ell\ \middle|\ \begin{aligned} a&=x_{2}x_{1}^{-1}x_{2}^{-1}x_{1},&\ell x_{2}\ell^{-1}&=x_{1},&[a,\ell]&=1,\\ &aba=bab,&aca=&cac,&\ell=(ab)&{}^{3}(ac)^{-3}\end{aligned}\right\rangle.

6=dimV=dimW≤dimW12+dimWa​b​c≤2+3​s.6=\dim V=\dim W\leq\dim W_{12}+\dim W_{abc}\leq 2+3s.

A12​B21=B21​A12=−N.A_{12}B_{21}=B_{21}A_{12}=-N.

6.2. Meridional rank of Wh⁡(S)\operatorname{Wh}(S)

We use group cohomology to give an estimate for mr⁡(Wh⁡(S))\operatorname{mr}(\operatorname{Wh}(S)). We recall the basic notions; see [14, 26] for general references. Let GG be a group and VV be a left GG-module. Functorially, Hn​(G,V):=Rn​Homℤ⁡[G]⁡(ℤ,V)H^{n}(G,V):=R^{n}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}[G]}(\mathbb{Z},V). Alternatively, the bar resolution gives a concrete cochain complex

where the maps are set theoretic, and the differential is given by

(d​f)​(g1,⋯,gn+1)=\displaystyle(df)(g_{1},\dotsb,g_{n+1})= g1⋅f⁡(g2,⋯,gn+1)+∑i=1n(−1)i​f​(g1,⋯,gi​gi+1,⋯,gn+1)\displaystyle g_{1}\cdot f(g_{2},\dotsb,g_{n+1})+\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^{i}f(g_{1},\dotsb,g_{i}g_{i+1},\dotsb,g_{n+1})
+(−1)n+1​f​(g1,⋯,gn).\displaystyle+(-1)^{n+1}f(g_{1},\dotsb,g_{n}).

We note two special cases. For n=0n=0,

H0​(G,V)=VG:={v∈V:ρ⁡(g)​v=v​ for every ​g∈G}.H^{0}(G,V)=V^{G}:=\{v\in V:\rho(g)v=v\text{ for every }g\in G\}.

For n=1n=1, the 1-cocycle maps are given by crossed homomorphisms:

Z1(G;V)={f:G→V:f(gh)=f(g)+ρ(g)f(h) for all g,h∈G},Z^{1}(G;V)=\{f:G\to V:f(gh)=f(g)+\rho(g)f(h)\text{ for all }g,h\in G\},

because (d​f)​(g,h)=g​f​(h)−f⁡(g​h)+f⁡(g)=0(df)(g,h)=gf(h)-f(gh)+f(g)=0. The 1-coboundary maps are given by principal crossed homomorphisms.

B1(G,V)={fv:v∈V,fv(g)=ρ(g)v−v},B^{1}(G,V)=\{f_{v}:v\in V,\ f_{v}(g)=\rho(g)v-v\},

because (d​v)​(g)=g​v−v(dv)(g)=gv-v.

Let GG be generated by r≥1r\geq 1 conjugates of an element mm, and let ρ:G→GL⁡(V)\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}(V) be a representation on a finite-dimensional vector space over a field 𝔽\mathbb{F}. Then

Let m1=mm_{1}=m and mi=gi−1​m​gim_{i}=g_{i}^{-1}mg_{i} for 2≤i≤r2\leq i\leq r. We have

(6.3) f⁡(mi)=f⁡(gi−1​m​gi)\displaystyle f(m_{i})=f(g_{i}^{-1}mg_{i}) =f⁡(gi−1)+ρ⁡(gi−1)​f​(m​gi)\displaystyle=f(g_{i}^{-1})+\rho(g_{i}^{-1})f(mg_{i})
(6.4) =−ρ⁡(gi−1)​f​(gi)+ρ⁡(gi−1)​(f⁡(m)+ρ⁡(m)​f​(gi))\displaystyle=-\rho(g_{i}^{-1})f(g_{i})+\rho(g_{i}^{-1})(f(m)+\rho(m)f(g_{i}))
(6.5) =ρ⁡(gi−1)​f​(m)+ρ⁡(gi−1)​(ρ⁡(m)−I)​f​(gi)\displaystyle=\rho(g_{i}^{-1})f(m)+\rho(g_{i}^{-1})(\rho(m)-I)f(g_{i})
(6.6) =ρ⁡(gi−1)​f​(m)+(ρ⁡(mi)−I)​ρ​(gi−1)​f​(gi).\displaystyle=\rho(g_{i}^{-1})f(m)+(\rho(m_{i})-I)\rho(g_{i}^{-1})f(g_{i}).

A cocycle is determined by its values on the generating set. Once f⁡(m)f(m) is fixed, the possible value of f⁡(mi)f(m_{i}) belongs to an affine space with direction im⁡((ρ⁡(mi)−I))\operatorname{im}((\rho(m_{i})-I)), the dimension of which equals to the microlocal rank. Therefore, the map

f\displaystyle f ⟼(f⁡(m),(f⁡(mi)−ρ⁡(gi−1)​f​(m))i=2r),\displaystyle\longmapsto\bigl(f(m),(f(m_{i})-\rho(g_{i}^{-1})f(m))_{i=2}^{r}\bigr),

is injective. Thus dimZ1​(G,V)≤dimV+(r−1)​μ​rk⁡(ρ)\dim Z^{1}(G;V)\leq\dim V+(r-1)\mu\operatorname{rk}(\rho), the inequality follows.

On the other hand, there is a short exact sequence 0→H0​(G,V)→V→B1​(G,V)→00\rightarrow H^{0}(G;V)\rightarrow V\rightarrow B^{1}(G;V)\rightarrow 0. This implies dimV=dimB1​(G,V)+dimH0​(G,V)\dim V=\dim B^{1}(G;V)+\dim H^{0}(G;V). ∎

Remark 6.3.

The left hand side of the inequality is in fact the truncated negative Euler number dimH1​(G,V)−dimH0​(G,V)\dim H^{1}(G,V)-\dim H^{0}(G,V). Indeed, there is a short exact sequence 0→H0​(G,V)→V→B1​(G,V)→00\rightarrow H^{0}(G,V)\rightarrow V\rightarrow B^{1}(G,V)\rightarrow 0. This implies dimV=dimB1​(G,V)+dimH0​(G,V)\dim V=\dim B^{1}(G,V)+\dim H^{0}(G,V). Therefore,

dimZ1​(G,V)−dimV=dimH1​(G,V)−dimH0​(G,V).\dim Z^{1}(G,V)-\dim V=\dim H^{1}(G,V)-\dim H^{0}(G,V).

It is straightforward to check these assignments satisfy the relators in πWh⁡(S)\pi_{\operatorname{Wh}(S)}, hence ϕ\phi is well defined.

Proposition 6.4.

ϕ\phi is surjective.

Proof.

Observe that

ϕ⁡(x1​b​c)=(1 6 5 14 3 4 11 9 10 13 7 2 12 8)\phi(x_{1}bc)=(1\,6\,5\,14\,3\,4\,11\,9\,10\,13\,7\,2\,12\,8)

is a cyclic permutation of order 1414, and

ϕ⁡((x2​b)7)=(1 13)\phi((x_{2}b)^{7})=(1\,13)

is a simple transposition. The distance between 1 and 13 in the cyclic permutation is 9, which is coprime to 14. Therefore these two elements generate S14S_{14}, proving surjectivity. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

We know that b⁡(Wh⁡(S))=6b(\operatorname{Wh}(S))=6, and that ar⁡(Wh⁡(S))≤5\operatorname{ar}(\operatorname{Wh}(S))\leq 5 by Proposition 6.1. If πW​h​(S)\pi_{Wh(S)} is generated by rr meridians, Lemma 6.2 and Proposition 6.5 imply

27−14=13≤3​(r−1).27-14=13\leq 3(r-1).

Hence r>5r>5. Together with the upper bound b=6b=6, this implies mr⁡(Wh⁡(S))=6\operatorname{mr}(\operatorname{Wh}(S))=6. ∎

Acknowledgements

The authors would like to thank Yu Zhao for some helpful conversations.

The authors acknowledge the use of OpenAI’s ChatGPT during the development of this work. This project began in October 2025, motivated in part by an interest in exploring how AI tools could support mathematical research. Initially, GPT assisted with writing SageMath code, implementing computations in SnapPy, and conducting computational experiments. It was later used to explore proof strategies, develop arguments, prepare an initial draft, and assist in checking the code, computations, and proposed proofs.

Throughout this process, the authors supplied the relevant literature, many of the initial mathematical ideas, detailed prompts, and directed the successive stages of experimentation, proof development, and revision. The initial AI-assisted draft was subsequently substantially rewritten by the authors, who reorganized the manuscript and revised the exposition and presentation of the proofs. Further checks and revisions were carried out through mathematical discussions among the authors and additional interactions with these tools. The AI-assisted checks were part of this review process, not an independent certification of the proofs. The authors take full responsibility for the mathematical content, computations, references, and final presentation.
